modules.title: Java Introduction
modules.goal: Java kya hai, kaise chalta hai, aur apna pehla program compile karke chalana.
prereqs: Programming ka koi experience zaroori nahi
objectives: Explain what Java is and why bytecode makes it platform independent
Tell JDK, JRE and JVM apart and say which one you install
Write, compile and run a Java program from the command line
Read a compiler error and fix the line it names
modules.definition: Java is a compiled, statically typed, object-oriented programming language. Source code (.java) is compiled by javac into bytecode (.class), which any JVM runs — so the same program works on Windows, Linux and macOS without recompiling.
explain: A program is a list of instructions: take input, store values, calculate, print a result. In Java those instructions live inside a class, and execution starts at a method with the exact signature public static void main(String[] args).

Java is compiled but not to machine code directly. javac turns your text into bytecode, a portable instruction set. The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) translates that bytecode for the machine it is running on. That extra step is why Java is called 'write once, run anywhere'.

Java is also statically typed: every variable has a type that is checked before the program runs. The compiler catches many mistakes that a Python program would only hit at runtime, which is a big reason large backends are written in Java.
hinglish: Simple words me: aap .java file me code likhte ho, javac usko .class bytecode me badalta hai, aur JVM us bytecode ko chalata hai. Isliye same .class file har OS par chalti hai — bas us machine par JVM hona chahiye.

Java me sab kuch class ke andar hota hai, aur program main() method se shuru hota hai. Type checking compile time par hoti hai, isliye galtiyan chalne se pehle pakdi jaati hain — bade backend systems isi wajah se Java choose karte hain.
modules.analogy: Java bytecode ek PDF file jaisa hai: aap ek hi PDF bhejte ho aur har device ka reader use khol leta hai. Machine code native video jaisa hai — sirf usi device par chalega. JVM har device ka PDF reader hai.
modules.why: Java backend engineering ki default language hai — banking, Android, big data (Kafka, Spark) aur enterprise services. Interviews me JVM, memory aur collections ke questions isi foundation se aate hain, aur Java ka OOP model baaki languages samajhne me bhi help karta hai.

syntax.note: public class Main file ka naam Main.java hona chahiye. main() entry point hai; String[] args command-line arguments rakhta hai.
Classes PascalCase, methods aur variables camelCase, constants UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. Comments compiler ignore karta hai.

topics.title: What is Java
topics.body: A general-purpose, class-based, object-oriented language designed for portability, readability and long-running services. It runs on the JVM, ships a huge standard library, and has automatic garbage collection.

topics.title: History in one minute
topics.body: James Gosling's team at Sun Microsystems released Java in 1995. Java 8 (2014) added lambdas and streams; Java 11, 17 and 21 are LTS releases. Java 21 is the LTS this course uses, with records, sealed classes and virtual threads — all final features, no preview flags.

topics.title: Features that matter
topics.body: Platform independence through bytecode, strong static typing, object orientation, automatic memory management, built-in multithreading, a rich standard library, and a mature ecosystem (Maven, Gradle, Spring).

topics.title: Java vs Python vs C++ vs JavaScript
topics.body: Python is interpreted, dynamically typed and shorter to write; Java is compiled to bytecode, statically typed and faster for large services. C++ compiles to native code and gives manual memory control. JavaScript runs in the browser and on Node.js. Java sits between raw speed and developer safety.

topics.title: JDK, JRE and JVM
topics.body: JVM runs bytecode. JRE = JVM + core libraries needed to run Java programs. JDK = JRE + compiler (javac) + tools needed to DEVELOP Java. You install the JDK; it contains everything else.

topics.title: Bytecode and the execution pipeline
topics.body: Main.java --javac--> Main.class (bytecode) --JVM--> machine instructions. The JVM verifies the bytecode, loads classes, and the JIT compiler turns hot methods into native code while the program runs.

topics.title: Install, JAVA_HOME and IDE
topics.body: Install an LTS JDK (Temurin 21, Oracle JDK 21 or your OS package). Set JAVA_HOME to the JDK folder and add its bin directory to PATH, then check with java -version and javac -version. Use IntelliJ IDEA Community, VS Code with the Java pack, or Eclipse.

topics.title: main(), comments and naming
topics.body: public static void main(String[] args) is the entry point: public so the JVM can call it, static so no object is needed, void because it returns nothing. Comments are // and /* */. Follow camelCase, PascalCase and UPPER_SNAKE_CASE conventions so other Java developers can read your code.

public static void main(String[] args) — the JVM looks for exactly this method to start the program.
System.out.println(...) — prints text and moves to a new line; System.out is the standard output stream.
The closing braces close main() first, then the class.

java Main starts the JVM with Main as the entry class.
The JVM calls main(), which prints two lines and returns.

examples.title: Command-line arguments and formatted output

The ternary expression picks args[0] or a default, so the program never crashes on no arguments.

The program prints one formatted line and exits.

mistakes.right: Put public class Student in Student.java

mistakes.wrong: public static void main() { }

best: Name the file after the public class — always.
Keep main short: parse input, call a method, print the result.
Run javac after small changes instead of writing 100 lines and then compiling.
Read compiler errors from the FIRST line: later errors are often caused by the first one.
modules.tip: Interviewers open with 'why is Java platform independent?' Answer with bytecode plus JVM, and add that the JVM itself is platform-specific — that second half is what separates a memorised answer from an understood one.
revision: JDK contains JRE contains JVM; you install the JDK.
javac compiles .java to .class bytecode; java runs it on the JVM.
Every Java program starts at public static void main(String[] args).
Classes are PascalCase, methods and variables camelCase, constants UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.

mcqs.q: Which command compiles Main.java?
mcqs.explain: javac compiles source to bytecode (Main.class); java runs the compiled class.

mcqs.q: What does the JVM actually execute?
mcqs.explain: javac produces bytecode in .class files; the JVM executes that bytecode.

mcqs.q: Which method signature is a valid Java entry point?
mcqs.explain: It must be public, static, void, and take a String[] parameter to be recognised by the JVM.

interview.q: Why is Java called platform independent?
interview.a: Because javac compiles source to a standard bytecode, and every platform runs that bytecode through its own JVM. The bytecode does not change; only the JVM implementation differs per operating system.
interview.followUp: Is the JVM itself platform independent? (No — each OS has its own JVM build.)

interview.q: What is the difference between JDK, JRE and JVM?
interview.a: The JVM executes bytecode. The JRE is the JVM plus the core libraries needed to run programs. The JDK is the JRE plus development tools such as javac, javadoc and jdb. Developers install the JDK.
interview.followUp: Which one would a production server need? (A JRE or a JDK with a runtime image; modern deployments often ship a custom jlink runtime.)

modules.title: Java Fundamentals
modules.goal: Variables, primitive types, operators, input/output aur type conversion ko confidently use karna.
prereqs: Module 01: a program that compiles and runs
objectives: Choose the right primitive type for a value
Predict the result of arithmetic, comparison and logical expressions
Read input with Scanner and format output with printf
Explain implicit conversion versus explicit casting
modules.definition: Java has eight primitive types (byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean) that store raw values, and reference types that store the address of an object. Variables are typed containers; operators combine values; Scanner reads input and System.out writes output.
explain: A variable is a named box with a fixed type. int holds whole numbers, double holds decimals, boolean holds true/false, char holds one character. The type decides how much memory the box takes and which operations are legal.

Java converts smaller types to larger ones automatically (int to long, int to double). Going the other way needs a cast, because information can be lost: (int) 9.7 becomes 9, not 10. Integer division also surprises beginners: 7 / 2 is 3, because both operands are int.

Scanner parses text from an input stream into typed values: nextInt(), nextDouble(), nextLine(). printf formats output with placeholders, which is how you print money, tables and aligned reports without manual padding.
hinglish: Variable ek dabba hai jiska type fix hota hai. int me pure number, double me decimal, boolean me true/false, char me ek character. Type se hi decide hota hai ki kaun se operations allowed hain.

Chhote type se bade type me conversion automatic hoti hai (int → double), bade se chhote me cast lagana padta hai aur data kat sakta hai. Aur haan: 7 / 2 Java me 3 hota hai, kyunki dono int hain — decimal chahiye to 7.0 / 2 likho.
modules.analogy: Types alag-alag size ke containers hain: byte ek chhoti dabbi, int ek normal box, long ek bada trunk, double ek measuring cup jisme decimals aate hain. Aap paani bade vessel me bina nuksan daal sakte ho, par chhoti dabbi me daalne se overflow ho jata hai.
modules.why: Every Java bug you will ever debug starts with a value of the wrong type, a wrong operator or a lost decimal. Getting these right makes later topics — methods, arrays, collections — dramatically easier, and numeric questions are a standard interview warm-up.

syntax.note: Literals: int is the default whole number, double the default decimal. Use L for long, f for float. final means the value cannot be reassigned.
Cast one operand to double to get decimal division. %.2f rounds to two decimals; %n is the newline.

topics.title: Variables and constants
topics.body: Declare with type name = value. A variable can be reassigned; a final variable cannot. Constants are final and conventionally UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. Local variables must be initialised before use.

topics.title: The eight primitive types
topics.body: byte (8-bit), short (16), int (32), long (64), float (32-bit decimal), double (64-bit decimal), char (16-bit Unicode), boolean. int and double cover most everyday work.

topics.title: Reference types
topics.body: String, arrays and objects store a reference to data, not the data itself. A reference can be null, which is why calling a method on an uninitialised object throws NullPointerException.

topics.title: Type conversion and casting
topics.body: Widening (int → long → double) is automatic. Narrowing (double → int) needs an explicit cast and truncates the fraction. Casting an out-of-range value wraps around, so validate before you cast.

topics.title: Operators
topics.body: Arithmetic + - * / %, relational == != < > <= >=, logical && || !, assignment = += -= *= /= %=, and increment/decrement ++ --. && and || short-circuit: the right side may not run.

topics.title: Precedence and integer division
topics.body: Multiplicative beats additive, comparison beats logical, and assignment comes last. Parenthesise when unsure. Division of two ints truncates; use a double operand for a decimal result.

topics.title: Scanner input
topics.body: new Scanner(System.in) reads tokens. nextInt() and nextDouble() leave the newline behind, so call nextLine() once after them before reading a full line. Close the scanner when done.

topics.title: Output and formatted output
topics.body: print writes without a newline, println adds one, printf formats with %d, %s, %f, %.2f, %b and %n. String.format returns the same text instead of printing it.

Widening is automatic, narrowing needs a cast.
Integer division truncates; cast an operand to double for decimals.
Scanner reads tokens; printf formats output with %d, %s, %.2f, %n.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 7 / 2 in Java?
mcqs.explain: Both operands are int, so integer division truncates to 3. Make one operand a double for 3.5.

mcqs.q: Which type stores a single character?
mcqs.explain: char holds one UTF-16 code unit in single quotes, e.g. 'A'. String is a reference type for text.

mcqs.q: What does (int) 9.99 produce?
mcqs.explain: Casting double to int truncates the fractional part; it does not round.

interview.q: What is the difference between primitive types and reference types?
interview.a: A primitive variable stores the value directly (int, double, boolean…). A reference variable stores the address of an object on the heap; the object itself lives elsewhere and the reference can be null.
interview.followUp: Where do primitives live? (As fields, with their object; as locals, in the stack frame. The language does not guarantee storage location — the JVM decides.)

interview.q: Why does == sometimes fail for Strings?
interview.a: For reference types == compares the reference, not the text. Two equal strings may be different objects, so use equals() to compare contents.
interview.followUp: When does == work for Strings? (For compile-time string literals that land in the string pool, which is an implementation detail, not a rule to rely on.)

modules.title: Strings
modules.goal: String immutability, pool, comparison aur StringBuilder ko theek se samajhna.
objectives: Explain why a String cannot be changed after creation
Choose between == and equals() and say what each compares
Use the common String methods without guessing their return values
Pick StringBuilder for repeated concatenation and say why
modules.definition: String is an immutable reference type representing a sequence of UTF-16 characters. Every method that appears to modify a String returns a new String. StringBuilder and StringBuffer are mutable alternatives used for repeated changes.
explain: A String is immutable: once created, its characters never change. Calling toUpperCase() returns a new String; the original is untouched. That sounds wasteful, but immutability makes strings safe to share, cache and use as HashMap keys.

Because equal string literals are shared in the string pool, two literals with the same text usually point at the same object, so == may look like it works. It does not compare text — it compares references. Always use equals() for content, and equalsIgnoreCase() when case should not matter.

When you concatenate inside a loop, each + creates a new String, which is O(n²) work. StringBuilder keeps a growable buffer and appends in place, so it is the right tool. StringBuffer is the thread-safe, slower sibling.
hinglish: String immutable hota hai: ek baar ban gaya to uske characters badal nahi sakte. toUpperCase() original ko nahi badalta, naya String return karta hai. Isi wajah se String ko safely share kar sakte ho aur HashMap ki key bana sakte ho.

String pool ki wajah se same literal wale strings ek hi object ko point kar sakte hain, isliye == kabhi kabhi sahi lagta hai — par wo text compare nahi karta, reference compare karta hai. Content compare karne ke liye hamesha equals() use karo. Loop me concatenation ke liye StringBuilder.
modules.analogy: String ek printed page jaisa hai: usme kuch badalna ho to naya page print hota hai, purana waisa hi rehta hai. StringBuilder ek whiteboard hai — usi board par likhte, mitate aur append karte ho, isliye baar-baar naya page nahi banta.
modules.why: Text is everywhere: names, JSON, logs, SQL, user input. String comparison bugs are among the most common production defects, and interviewers ask about immutability and the pool in almost every Java screening.

syntax.note: Use equals() for content. length() is a method on String (arrays use the length field).
append returns the same builder, so calls chain. toString() gives you the finished String.

topics.title: Creating strings
topics.body: A literal ("Java") reuses the string pool. new String("Java") forces a fresh heap object. Prefer literals: they are cheaper and easier to compare correctly with equals().

topics.title: Immutability
topics.body: charAt, substring, replace, trim and toUpperCase all return new Strings. This makes strings thread-safe, hashable and safe to share, at the cost of extra objects when you modify repeatedly.

topics.title: String pool and interning
topics.body: The JVM caches literal strings in a pool so identical literals share one object. intern() returns the pooled instance. Do not rely on pooling for correctness — compare with equals().

topics.title: equals() versus ==
topics.body: == compares references (or primitive values). equals() compares content when the class overrides it, as String does. Use Objects.equals(a, b) when either side may be null, or "literal".equals(variable) to avoid a NullPointerException.

topics.title: The methods you actually use
topics.body: length, charAt, substring(begin, end), indexOf, contains, startsWith, endsWith, replace, split, trim, strip, toLowerCase, toUpperCase, isEmpty, isBlank, repeat, join, valueOf.

topics.title: Concatenation, StringBuilder and StringBuffer
topics.body: The compiler turns a single expression's + into a StringBuilder internally, but a loop of + creates a builder per iteration. StringBuilder is mutable and fast, not thread-safe; StringBuffer synchronises every method and is slower.

topics.title: Formatting, parsing and Character
topics.body: String.format and printf share placeholders. Integer.parseInt, Double.parseDouble and String.valueOf convert between text and numbers; a malformed value throws NumberFormatException. Character.isDigit, isLetter, isUpperCase and toUpperCase handle single characters.

examples.title: Clean a name and compare it safely
lines: trim() removes leading and trailing spaces, not the space in the middle, so the name is 10 characters.
split(" ") cuts on a single space and returns two parts: aman and kumar.
startsWith checks the prefix of the cleaned name.

examples.title: Reverse with StringBuilder
lines: new StringBuilder(word) copies the characters into a mutable buffer.
reverse() reverses that buffer in place and returns it.
toString() produces the final String, which is compared with equals.
Both strings have seven characters, so the length comparison is true.

mistakes.wrong: if (role == "admin") { }
mistakes.right: if ("admin".equals(role)) { }
mistakes.why: == compares references, so a role read from input or built at runtime may be a different object. The literal-first form is also null-safe.

mistakes.wrong: String s = ""; for (String w : words) s += w + ",";
mistakes.right: StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); for (String w : words) sb.append(w).append(',');
mistakes.why: Each += creates a new String, so the loop allocates O(n²) characters. StringBuilders append in place.

debug.brief: This program prints 'different' even though both words are Java. Fix the comparison.
hints: What does == compare for reference types?
equals() compares the characters.

best: Compare text with equals(); put the literal first when the other side may be null.
Use StringBuilder inside loops, String for values that do not change.
Use isBlank() rather than trim().isEmpty() to detect whitespace-only input.
Never build SQL or JSON by concatenating user input — use parameters and libraries.
modules.tip: When asked 'why is String immutable?', give three consequences: safe sharing and pooling, safe hash keys, and thread safety without locks. Then mention that this is why string concatenation in a loop is expensive.
revision: Strings are immutable; methods return new Strings.
== compares references, equals() compares content.
StringBuilder for repeated changes, StringBuffer when shared across threads.
parseInt/parseDouble convert text, String.valueOf converts values to text.

mcqs.q: What does "Java".substring(1) return?
mcqs.explain: substring(1) starts at index 1 and goes to the end, so it returns ava.

mcqs.q: Which comparison checks the characters of two Strings?
mcqs.explain: equals() compares content for String; == compares references.

mcqs.explain: String concatenation creates a new object each time; StringBuilder mutates one buffer.

interview.q: What is the String constant pool?
interview.a: A JVM-managed area where identical string literals are stored once and reused. new String("x") creates a separate heap object, which is why == can fail while equals() succeeds.
interview.followUp: What does intern() do? (Returns the pooled instance for that text.)

interview.q: StringBuilder vs StringBuffer?
interview.a: Both are mutable. StringBuilder is faster and not thread-safe; StringBuffer synchronises its methods, so it is safe across threads but slower. Use StringBuilder unless the buffer is genuinely shared.
interview.followUp: Is String concatenation with + always slow? (No — a single expression compiles to one StringBuilder; only repeated concatenation in a loop is the problem.)

modules.title: Conditional Statements
modules.goal: if, else-if, switch aur modern switch expressions se decisions lena.
objectives: Write an if / else-if chain whose branches are mutually exclusive
Use a switch statement and a switch expression correctly
Choose the ternary operator for a single expression, not for side effects
Avoid fall-through and assignment-in-condition bugs
modules.definition: Conditional statements choose which block runs based on a boolean expression. Java has if/else, switch statements (with explicit break or arrow labels), switch expressions that return a value, and the ternary operator for a two-way choice inside an expression.
explain: An if statement evaluates a boolean and runs its block only when that boolean is true. else runs when it is false, and else-if chains let you test conditions in order — the first true branch wins, and the rest are skipped.

A switch compares one value against constant labels. Old-style labels need break, otherwise execution falls through into the next case. Arrow labels (case 1 -> ...) never fall through. A switch expression must produce a value on every path, which the compiler checks — a default branch or an exhaustive enum keeps it safe.
Conditions should read like a rule: check the invalid cases first and return early, then handle the happy path. That keeps nesting shallow and makes each branch obvious.
hinglish: if me boolean expression decide karta hai kaunsa block chalega. else-if chain me pehla true branch jeetta hai aur baaki skip ho jaate hain — isliye order matter karta hai.

Switch ek value ko constant labels se compare karta hai. Purane style me break bhoolne par fall-through ho jata hai; arrow labels me fall-through nahi hota. Switch expression har path par value deta hai, aur compiler usko check karta hai.
modules.analogy: Conditions railway junction hain: signal (boolean) decide karta hai train kaunsi patti par jaayegi. else-if chain ek sequence of signals hai — pehla green signal milte hi train aage badh jaati hai, baaki signals dekhe hi nahi jaate.
modules.why: Every real program validates input and branches on state: login success or failure, grade bands, discount rules, HTTP status handling. Getting branch order and boundaries right is the difference between a correct report and a silent off-by-one.

syntax.note: Order matters: check the highest band first. Once a branch matches, the rest are skipped.
A switch expression returns a value. Arrow labels never fall through; default makes it exhaustive for any int.

topics.title: if, else and else-if
topics.body: A boolean expression in parentheses, then a block. else-if chains are evaluated top to bottom; put the narrowest or highest-priority case first so it is not swallowed by a broader one.

topics.title: Nested conditions and early return
topics.body: Nesting is sometimes necessary, but guard clauses usually read better: test the invalid case, return or throw, then continue with the normal path at the top level of the method.

topics.title: Switch statements
topics.body: Switch works on int-compatible types, String, enums and (with patterns) reference types. Classic cases need break to avoid fall-through. Multiple labels can share a branch with case 1, 2, 3:.

topics.title: Modern switch expressions
topics.body: case X -> value has no fall-through and returns a value. Use yield inside a block when the branch needs several statements. The compiler enforces exhaustiveness, so an enum switch with every constant needs no default.

topics.title: Ternary and logical conditions
topics.body: condition ? a : b chooses one of two values. && requires both sides true and short-circuits; || needs one true and also short-circuits; ! negates. Prefer && and || over bitwise & and | in conditions.

topics.title: Boundaries and real-world rules
topics.body: Write the edge values down: 59/60, 0, negative, null, empty string. Then test those with a quick main. Most conditional bugs are boundary bugs or a missing invalid-input branch.

examples.title: Grade bands with else-if
lines: 78 >= 90 is false, so the first branch is skipped.
78 >= 75 is true, so the B branch runs.
Because a branch already ran, the remaining else-if tests are skipped.
The else acts as the fallback for every lower mark.

examples.title: Switch expression over a code
examples.output:
PRIORITY ships in 2 days
Fast track
lines: The switch expression matches PRIORITY and produces 2.
days receives that value; default guarantees a result for any other code.
The concatenation builds the first output line.
The ternary checks days <= 2 and prints Fast track.

mistakes.wrong: switch (day) { case 1: System.out.println("Mon"); case 2: System.out.println("Tue"); }
mistakes.right: switch (day) { case 1 -> System.out.println("Mon"); case 2 -> System.out.println("Tue"); }
mistakes.why: Classic cases fall through without break, so day 1 prints both lines. Arrow labels do not fall through.

mistakes.wrong: if (marks >= 60) { ... } else if (marks >= 90) { ... }
mistakes.right: if (marks >= 90) { ... } else if (marks >= 60) { ... }
mistakes.why: The highest band must be tested first; otherwise a mark of 95 matches >= 60 and the A branch is unreachable.

debug.brief: This menu should print Only tea for choice 1, but prints both lines. Fix the switch.
hints: Execution falls into the next case when a case does not end.
Add break after each classic case, or switch to arrow labels.

best: Check invalid or empty input first, then the normal path (guard clauses).
Prefer switch expressions when every branch produces a value.
Keep conditions as named booleans when the expression is long.
Test boundaries explicitly: 0, 1, max, max + 1, and the exact pass mark.
modules.tip: Interviewers often ask for a switch on an enum with no default. The correct answer is a switch expression over all constants: the compiler proves exhaustiveness, and adding a new constant becomes a compile error instead of a silent bug.
revision: First matching branch wins; order bands from highest to lowest.
Classic switch falls through without break; arrow labels never do.
Switch expressions return a value and must be exhaustive.
Ternary picks a value; do not hide side effects inside it.

practice.title: Leap year
practice.prompt: Read a year and print Leap or Not leap using the divisible-by-4/100/400 rule.

practice.title: Largest of three
practice.prompt: Read three integers and print the largest without using Math.max.
practice.hint: Compare a against b, then the winner against c.

practice.title: Menu with switch expression
practice.prompt: Map codes 1-3 to Starter, Main and Dessert; print Unknown for anything else, using a switch expression.
practice.hint: case 1 -> "Starter"; … default -> "Unknown";

mcqs.q: What happens when a classic switch case has no break?
options: Execution falls through into the next case
mcqs.explain: Without break, control continues into the following case's statements.

mcqs.q: Which operator must guard a nullable String before calling equals on it?
mcqs.explain: Calling value.equals(...) on null throws; a literal-first equals returns false safely.

mcqs.q: A switch expression over all enum constants without a default…
mcqs.explain: The compiler verifies that every enum constant is covered, so no default is required.

interview.q: switch vs if-else — when do you choose which?
interview.a: Switch is clearer and faster for equality against a fixed set of constants (enums, codes). if-else handles ranges and compound boolean conditions. With switch expressions the compiler also checks exhaustiveness, which is a correctness win.
interview.followUp: What types can switch on? (int-compatible types, String, enums; patterns extend this in modern Java.)

interview.q: What is fall-through and when is it intentional?
interview.a: Fall-through is execution continuing into the next case because there is no break. It is occasionally used to share setup between several labels, but arrow labels or deliberate grouped labels are clearer and safer.
interview.followUp: How do arrow labels change it? (They never fall through, and each branch is its own scope.)

lab.title: Grade calculator
lab.brief: Read marks (0-100). Print A for 90+, B for 75+, C for 60+, D for 40+, else F. Print Invalid for values outside 0-100.
hints: Check the invalid range before the grade bands.
Test the highest band first.

checkpoint.title: Decisions clear?
checks: I order else-if bands so no branch is unreachable
I know why classic switch needs break and arrow labels do not
I tested the boundary values, not just the happy path

modules.title: Loops
modules.goal: for, while, do-while, nested loops aur break/continue par command.
objectives: Choose for, while or do-while for a given repetition
Trace a nested loop and predict how many times the body runs
Use break and continue without creating unreadable control flow
Recognise and fix an infinite loop
modules.definition: A loop repeats a block while a condition holds. for groups initialisation, condition and update in one line; while checks before each iteration; do-while checks after, so it always runs at least once. break exits the loop, continue skips to the next iteration.
explain: Use for when you know how many times to repeat or you are walking an index range. Use while when the repetition depends on something that changes inside the loop, such as reading until input ends. Use do-while when the body must run at least once, like showing a menu before checking whether the user wants to quit.

Nested loops multiply: an outer loop of n iterations with an inner loop of m iterations runs the inner body n × m times. That is exactly how pattern printing works, and also why an accidental n² loop on 100,000 items is a performance bug.

An infinite loop happens when the condition never becomes false. Common causes: forgetting to update the counter, updating in the wrong direction, or a condition that can never be true. Add a print or a debugger breakpoint inside the loop to see the variable that is not moving.
hinglish: Jab repetitions ki count pata ho ya index ke saath kaam ho, for loop use karo. Jab condition kuch andar badalne par depend kare, while. Aur jab body kam se kam ek baar chalni hi chahiye, do-while — jaise menu pehle dikhana, phir poochna ki quit karna hai kya.

Nested loop me kaam multiply hota hai: outer n baar, inner m baar → body n × m baar. Patterns isi se bante hain. Aur infinite loop tab hota hai jab counter update hi nahi hota ya galat direction me hota hai — loop ke andar variable print karke dekho.
modules.analogy: Loop ek gym circuit jaisa hai: for me aapko pata hai 3 rounds karne hain; while me aap tab tak karte ho jab tak energy hai; do-while me aap pehle ek round karte ho, phir decide karte ho ki aur karna hai ya nahi.
modules.why: Loops are how programs process collections, files and user input. Pattern questions and complexity questions in interviews both assume you can trace a nested loop precisely — and most infinite-loop incidents in production come from a condition that never changes.

syntax.note: for declares its counter in the loop; while needs the variable outside; do-while always runs once.
continue jumps to the update step of a for loop; break leaves the loop entirely.

topics.title: The for loop
topics.body: for (init; condition; update). Initialisation runs once, condition is checked before each iteration, update runs after the body. Declare the counter inside the parentheses unless you need it after the loop.

topics.title: while and do-while
topics.body: while may run zero times. do-while runs the body first and then checks, so it runs at least once — the usual shape for a menu or a retry loop.

topics.title: Nested loops
topics.body: The inner loop finishes completely for each outer iteration. Row and column loops print grids; two independent nested loops over n give O(n²) work, which matters as data grows.

topics.title: break and continue
topics.body: break exits the nearest loop (or switch). continue skips the rest of the current iteration. Both affect only the innermost loop — to leave two levels, use a labelled break, which should be rare and clearly commented.

topics.title: Patterns
topics.body: Star and number patterns are nested loops with a formula per row: print spaces, then symbols, then a newline. Writing the row formula on paper first is faster than guessing in code.

topics.title: Infinite loops and debugging
topics.body: If a loop never ends, check that the update actually changes the condition variable and moves toward the exit. A for(;;) loop is legal and is sometimes intentional with a break; an accidental while(true) is a bug.

examples.title: Multiplication table
lines: table holds the value being multiplied; i is the loop counter.
The condition i <= 5 keeps the loop running for i = 1..5.
The body prints one line per iteration; the multiplication is in parentheses so it happens before concatenation.
i++ moves toward the exit condition.

examples.title: Star triangle with nested loops
lines: The outer loop controls the row number r, from 1 to 4.
The inner loop prints exactly r stars, because its condition is c <= r.
print writes stars without a newline; println after the inner loop ends the row.
Total stars printed: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

mistakes.wrong: for (int i = 0; i < 5; i--) { }
mistakes.right: for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { }
mistakes.why: The counter moves away from the exit condition, so the loop never ends.

mistakes.wrong: for (int i = 0; i <= arr.length; i++) sum += arr[i];
mistakes.right: for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) sum += arr[i];
mistakes.why: The last valid index is length - 1. Using <= reads past the end and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

debug.brief: This loop should print 1 to 5 but never stops. Fix the update.
hints: Which direction is the counter moving?
It must move toward 6 to make the condition false.

best: Prefer for-each (`for (int x : nums)`) when you do not need the index.
Keep the loop body to one job; extract a method if it grows.
Avoid changing the counter inside the body — it makes tracing much harder.
If a loop needs a comment to explain its exit condition, rewrite the condition.
modules.tip: A classic interview question is 'how many times does this nested loop run?'. Count outer iterations × inner iterations, then state the complexity: n × m, or O(n²) when both are n. Show the arithmetic, do not just say 'n squared'.
revision: for = known count, while = condition-driven, do-while = at least once.
Nested loops multiply their iteration counts.
break exits the nearest loop; continue skips one iteration.
An infinite loop means the condition variable never reaches its exit value.

practice.title: Sum 1 to n
practice.prompt: Read n and print the sum 1 + 2 + … + n with a loop, then check it against n*(n+1)/2.
practice.hint: Accumulate in an int/long; for n up to 10^9 use long or the formula.

practice.title: Reverse a table
practice.prompt: Print the 5 times table from 10 down to 1 using a single for loop.
practice.hint: Start at 10 and decrement.

practice.title: Pyramid
practice.prompt: Print a centred pyramid of stars for n rows: spaces, then stars, then a newline.
practice.hint: Row r needs n-r spaces and 2r-1 stars.

mcqs.q: How many times does the body run? for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)
mcqs.explain: i takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3 — four iterations.

mcqs.q: Which loop always executes its body at least once?
mcqs.explain: do-while checks its condition after the body, so the first pass always happens.

mcqs.q: What does continue do inside a for loop?
mcqs.explain: continue skips the remaining body and jumps to the loop's update expression.

interview.q: What is the time complexity of two nested loops over n items?
interview.a: O(n²) when the inner loop also runs up to n times, because the inner body executes n × n times. If the inner loop runs a constant number of times, the whole thing is still O(n).
interview.followUp: How do you make it faster? (Use a hash structure to replace the inner search, turning it into O(n) average time.)

interview.q: How would you break out of two nested loops?
interview.a: Use a labelled break (outer: for … { break outer; }), or refactor so the inner work is a method that returns a boolean. The labelled break works but is easy to misread; extraction is usually clearer.
interview.followUp: Why does an unlabelled break not work? (It exits only the innermost loop or switch.)

lab.title: Sum of first n numbers
lab.brief: Read a positive integer n and print the sum 1 + 2 + … + n using a loop.
hints: Keep an int sum starting at 0.
Use long if you test values above 65,535 — the sum grows fast.
