checks: I can pick for, while or do-while and justify it
I can count nested-loop iterations without running the code
I have fixed an infinite loop by finding the counter that did not move

modules.title: Number Logic and Recursion
modules.goal: Prime, palindrome, fibonacci jaise number problems aur recursion ka call stack.
objectives: Test primality in O(sqrt n) and explain why that is enough
Solve digit problems with division and modulo
Write a recursive method with a correct base case
Trace the call stack of a recursive method and compare it with iteration
modules.definition: Number logic problems manipulate digits and divisors with loops and modulo. Recursion is a method calling itself on a smaller input, with a base case that stops the calls; each pending call waits on the stack until the smaller calls return.
explain: Most number problems are digit arithmetic: n % 10 gives the last digit, n / 10 removes it. Repeating that pair lets you sum digits, reverse a number, or check a palindrome without converting to text.

Primality only needs divisors up to the square root: if n = a × b and both factors were bigger than sqrt(n), their product would exceed n. Checking 2 and then odd numbers up to sqrt(n) is enough — and it is the difference between a solution that passes and one that times out.

Recursion splits a problem into a smaller copy of itself. factorial(5) needs factorial(4), which needs factorial(3), down to factorial(0) — the base case. Without a base case the calls never stop and the stack overflows. Each waiting call keeps its own local variables, which is exactly what the call stack picture shows.
hinglish: Number problems me do operations ka jodi kaam karti hai: n % 10 last digit deta hai, n / 10 usse hata deta hai. Isse digit sum, reverse aur palindrome bina String banaye ho jaate hain.

Prime check ke liye sirf sqrt(n) tak divide dekhna kaafi hai: agar n = a × b aur dono sqrt(n) se bade ho, to product n se bada ho jaayega. Recursion me base case sabse zaroori hai — bina uske StackOverflowError aata hai, kyunki har call apna frame stack par rakhti hai.
modules.analogy: Recursion Russian dolls jaisa hai: sabse chhoti doll (base case) milte hi aap wapas bade dolls band karte ho. Har doll ke andar wali doll ka result bahar wali ko chahiye, isliye sab frames stack par wait karte hain.
modules.why: Placement tests and interviews are full of number and recursion questions because they test loops, boundaries and the call stack at once. Recursion also underpins trees, graphs, divide-and-conquer and the Stream API's reduce.

syntax.note: (long) d * d avoids int overflow near Integer.MAX_VALUE. Returning early keeps the loop simple.
Every recursive method needs a base case and an argument that moves toward it.

topics.title: Prime numbers
topics.body: n is prime when it has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself. Handle n < 2 first, then test divisors from 2 to sqrt(n). Checking every number up to n - 1 is correct but too slow for large inputs.

topics.title: Palindrome, Armstrong and perfect numbers
topics.body: A palindrome number reads the same reversed. An Armstrong number equals the sum of its digits each raised to the number of digits (153 = 1³ + 5³ + 3³). A perfect number equals the sum of its proper divisors (6 = 1 + 2 + 3). All three are digit/divisor loops.

topics.title: Fibonacci and factorial
topics.body: Fibonacci: each term is the sum of the previous two, with 0 and 1 as seeds. Factorial: n! = n × (n-1)!, with 0! = 1. Iterative versions use O(1) extra space; naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes the same values exponentially.

topics.title: GCD and LCM
topics.body: Euclid's algorithm: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b is 0. lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b — divide first to reduce overflow risk. Both are short enough to memorise and are asked often.

topics.title: Digits: sum, count and reverse
topics.body: While n > 0: digit = n % 10, then n /= 10. Accumulate sum, count or reversed = reversed * 10 + digit. Negative inputs need Math.abs or a sign flag; zero needs its own handling in some problems.

topics.title: Recursion, base cases and the stack
topics.body: A recursive call pushes a frame holding parameters and locals; returning pops it. The base case stops the descent. Too deep a recursion throws StackOverflowError — that is a design limit, not a random crash.

topics.title: Recursion versus iteration
topics.body: Recursion is clearer for trees, divide-and-conquer and backtracking. Iteration is cheaper in memory and avoids stack limits for simple loops. Anything recursive can be rewritten iteratively with an explicit stack.

examples.title: Prime check up to sqrt(n)
lines: isPrime rejects everything below 2, which handles 0, 1 and negatives in one check.
The loop stops at sqrt(n) because a larger divisor would need a matching factor below it.
9 is divisible by 3, 25 by 5, so both return false early.
17 has no divisor up to 4, so it returns true.
dryRun: n = 17: d = 2, 3, 4 → no divisor; loop ends → true
Each result is printed with its verdict

examples.title: Recursive factorial and its call stack
lines: factorial(5) cannot multiply until factorial(4) returns, so five frames stack up.
factorial(1) hits the base case and returns 1 without another call.
factorial(0) also returns 1, because the base case is n <= 1.

mistakes.wrong: for (int d = 2; d < n; d++) if (n % d == 0) return false;
mistakes.right: for (int d = 2; (long) d * d <= n; d++) if (n % d == 0) return false;
mistakes.why: Checking every divisor is O(n) and times out; sqrt(n) is enough. Casting to long prevents overflow when squaring.

mistakes.wrong: static int fact(int n) { return n * fact(n - 1); }
mistakes.right: static int fact(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n * fact(n - 1); }
mistakes.why: Without a base case the recursion never stops and the stack overflows.

debug.brief: This factorial should print 120 but crashes with StackOverflowError. Add the missing base case.
hints: What should factorial return when n reaches 1?
Stop the recursion before it goes below 1.

best: Validate the input at the top: negative, zero and 1 break naive digit loops.
Use long for factorial, Fibonacci and sums that grow quickly.
Memoise or iterate for Fibonacci; the naive recursion is exponential.
Write the base case first, then the recursive step, then trace n = 0, 1, 2.
modules.tip: When you write a recursive answer in an interview, say the base case, the recursive relation and the stack depth out loud. Interviewers are checking that you know why it terminates, not just that it compiles.
revision: Prime check only needs divisors up to sqrt(n).
Digits: % 10 peels the last digit, / 10 removes it.
Euclid: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a % b).
Recursion needs a base case and an argument that shrinks.

practice.title: Armstrong numbers
practice.prompt: Print all Armstrong numbers between 1 and 999 (for example 153).
practice.hint: Count digits, then sum digit^count.

practice.title: GCD and LCM
practice.prompt: Read two integers and print their GCD and LCM on two lines.
practice.hint: lcm = a / gcd * b; use long for the multiplication.

practice.title: Recursive sum of digits
practice.prompt: Write sumDigits(n) recursively and print sumDigits(9876).
practice.hint: Base case n == 0 → 0; else n % 10 + sumDigits(n / 10).

mcqs.q: Why is it enough to test divisors up to sqrt(n)?
options: Because any factor pair has one factor <= sqrt(n)
mcqs.explain: If n = a × b with a <= b, then a <= sqrt(n); testing up to sqrt(n) finds every composite.

mcqs.q: What happens if a recursive method has no base case?
options: It compiles but throws StackOverflowError at runtime
mcqs.explain: Each call pushes a frame until the stack is exhausted; the JVM throws StackOverflowError.

mcqs.q: What does 153 % 10 give?
mcqs.explain: % is the remainder: 153 divided by 10 leaves 3.

interview.q: How would you improve a naive recursive Fibonacci?
interview.a: Naive recursion is O(2ⁿ) because it recomputes the same subproblems. Memoise results in an array or map for O(n), or iterate with two variables for O(n) time and O(1) space.
interview.followUp: What is the space complexity of the recursive version? (O(n) stack depth.)

interview.q: When would you choose recursion over a loop?
interview.a: When the data is naturally recursive — trees, nested structures, divide-and-conquer, backtracking — because the code mirrors the structure. For simple repetition, a loop is cheaper and avoids stack limits.
interview.followUp: How do you convert recursion to iteration? (Keep an explicit stack or track the state in variables.)

lab.title: Reverse the digits
lab.brief: Read an integer and print its digits reversed. Keep the sign for negative numbers (for example -123 → -321).
hints: Take the sign out first with Math.abs, then put it back.
reversed = reversed * 10 + n % 10; n /= 10.

checkpoint.title: Numbers and recursion rehearsed?
checks: I can explain the sqrt(n) bound for primality
I can trace a recursive method's stack down to its base case
I handled negative and zero inputs in a digit problem

modules.title: Methods
modules.goal: Methods likhna, parameters pass karna, return values aur overloading samajhna.
objectives: Declare and call a method with parameters and a return value
Explain why Java passes arguments by value, including object references
Overload a method on purpose, not by accident
Decide between static and instance methods
modules.definition: A method is a named block of code with a parameter list and a return type. Calling it runs the block with the arguments you pass. void means it returns nothing. Overloading means several methods share a name but differ in parameter types or count.
explain: Methods turn a long main into named steps. A method signature is the name plus the parameter types; that is what the compiler uses to pick the right method. The return type is not part of the signature, which is why two methods cannot differ only by return type.

Java is strictly pass-by-value. For primitives, the method receives a copy of the value. For objects, it receives a copy of the reference — so the method can change the object's state, but cannot make the caller's variable point at a different object.

A static method belongs to the class and is called without an object; an instance method belongs to an object and can read its fields. Overloading lets println handle ints, doubles and Strings with one name; the compiler chooses the version from the argument types at compile time.
hinglish: Method lambi main ko named steps me todta hai. Signature = name + parameter types; compiler isi se decide karta hai kaunsa method chalega. Return type signature ka part nahi hai, isliye sirf return type badal kar overload nahi kar sakte.

Java pass-by-value hai. Primitive ki copy jaati hai; object ka reference copy hota hai — matlab method object ka state badal sakta hai, par caller ka variable kisi naye object ko point nahi karwa sakta. static method class ka hota hai, instance method object ka.
modules.analogy: Method ek kitchen appliance jaisa hai: input daalo (arguments), button dabao (call), output lo (return value). Same appliance ke alag-alag attachments (overloading) ho sakte hain — naam ek, kaam input ke type se decide hota hai.
modules.why: Methods are the unit of reuse, testing and readability. Every framework you will use — JUnit, Spring, Streams — is built on method calls, and interviewers judge your code by whether it is decomposed into small, named, testable methods.

syntax.note: static methods are called by class name (or directly inside the same class). void methods are called for their effect, not a value.
Overloads must differ in parameter types or count. Choosing a boolean flag to distinguish a circle is a design smell — a separate method name is clearer.

topics.title: Declaration, call and signature
topics.body: A declaration names the method, its parameters and its return type. A call supplies arguments that must be assignable to the parameter types. Signature = name + parameter types; return type alone cannot overload.

topics.title: Parameters, arguments and return values
topics.body: Parameters are the variables in the declaration; arguments are the values at the call site. A non-void method must return a value of its declared type on every path, which the compiler checks.

topics.title: void methods
topics.body: A void method performs an effect — printing, updating an object, saving a file. It can still use return; with no value to exit early. Prefer returning a value and printing at the call site when you want the method testable.

topics.title: Method overloading
topics.body: Same name, different parameter lists. The compiler picks the most specific applicable overload. Beware ambiguity with null arguments and autoboxing: overloads that differ only by Integer versus int can surprise you.

topics.title: static versus instance
topics.body: Static methods belong to the class and cannot touch instance fields directly. Instance methods belong to an object and can read or change its state. Utility functions are static; behaviour tied to data is an instance method.

topics.title: Scope and varargs
topics.body: A parameter and any local declared in a block exist only in that block. Varargs (String... names) accepts zero or more arguments and arrives as an array, so it must be the last parameter.

topics.title: Recursion through methods
topics.body: A method may call itself or another method that calls back. Recursion is method calls on the stack; the base case and the shrinking argument are what make it terminate.

examples.title: Overloaded area, chosen by argument types
lines: The first overload takes one int: a square's area.
The second takes two ints: a rectangle's area.
area(4) matches the one-parameter version, so it returns 16.
area(4, 5) matches the two-parameter version and returns 20.
dryRun: println prints each result on its own line

examples.title: Varargs and a value-returning method
lines: int... marks accepts any number of ints and exposes them as an array.
The empty case returns 0 before dividing, so there is no divide-by-zero.
The cast to double makes the division produce a decimal.
printf formats the first result to two decimals; println prints 0.0 for the empty call.

mistakes.wrong: static void add(int a, int b) { int sum = a + b; }
mistakes.right: static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
mistakes.why: The sum is a local that disappears when the method returns. Return it, or the caller gets nothing.

mistakes.wrong:
static int area(int side) { return side * side; }
static double area(int side) { return side * side; }
mistakes.right: Use different names, or different parameter lists.
mistakes.why: Return type is not part of the signature, so these two declarations are a duplicate-method compile error.

debug.brief: This method should return the larger number but does not compile. Fix it.
hints: What does the method return when a is not greater than b?
A non-void method must return on every path.

best: One method, one job; name it after what it returns or does.
Prefer returning a value over printing inside the method — it is testable.
Keep parameter lists short; a long list usually wants an object.
Do not overload with boolean flags to switch behaviour — use a clearer name.
modules.tip: A standard screen question is 'is Java pass-by-reference?'. Say no, explain pass-by-value with an object reference, and give the swap example: swapping two object references inside a method does not affect the caller.
revision: Signature = name + parameter types; return type is not part of it.
Java passes everything by value; objects pass a copy of the reference.
Overloading is compile-time; overriding is runtime.
Varargs must be the last parameter and arrives as an array.

practice.title: Calculator methods
practice.prompt: Write add, subtract, multiply and divide methods returning double, then call them from main.
practice.hint: Guard division by zero before dividing.

practice.title: Overloaded greet
practice.prompt: Write greet(String) and greet(String, int) where the second repeats the greeting n times.
practice.hint: Loop inside the two-argument overload.

practice.title: Prime method
practice.prompt: Extract the prime check from module 06 into isPrime(int) and call it for 1 to 20.
practice.hint: Return a boolean; print at the call site.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT part of a method signature?
mcqs.explain: The signature is the name plus parameter types. Return type is not part of it for overload resolution.

mcqs.q: What does a void method return?
mcqs.explain: void means no value is returned; a bare return; only exits early.

mcqs.q: Java parameter passing is…
mcqs.explain: Java always passes values. For objects, the value is a copy of the reference.

interview.q: Can you overload a method by changing only its return type?
interview.a: No. The compiler resolves overloads from the name and parameter types; return type alone produces a duplicate-method error. Change the parameter list or the method name.
interview.followUp: Can you overload with varargs? (Yes, but it can create ambiguity with fixed-arity overloads; the compiler prefers the fixed version.)

interview.q: What is the difference between static and instance methods?
interview.a: Static methods belong to the class, have no this reference and cannot access instance fields directly. Instance methods belong to an object and can read and modify its state. Utility code is static; behaviour over data is an instance method.
interview.followUp: Can a static method call an instance method directly? (Not without an object.)

lab.title: Largest of three, with a method
lab.brief: Read three integers and print the largest one using a max3 method — not Math.max.
hints: Find the max of a and b, then compare that with c.
Return the answer from the method and print in main.

checkpoint.title: Methods in your hands?
checks: I can declare a method with parameters and a return value
I can explain pass-by-value with an object reference
I know why two methods cannot differ only by return type

modules.title: Arrays
modules.goal: Arrays declare, traverse, search, sort aur 2D arrays handle karna.
objectives: Declare, initialise and traverse one- and two-dimensional arrays
Explain the difference between an array's length field and a String's length()
Search and sort an array with a loop and with java.util.Arrays
Read and fix an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
modules.definition: An array is a fixed-size container of values of one type, stored contiguously and accessed by a zero-based index. Its length is fixed at creation. A two-dimensional array is an array of arrays, so its rows may have different lengths (a jagged array).
explain: Arrays give you numbered slots. int[] marks = new int[5] creates five ints initialised to 0; the valid indexes are 0 to 4. Asking for marks[5] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, because the last valid index is always length - 1.

Traversal is a loop from 0 to length - 1, or a for-each loop when you only need the values. For-each cannot change the array elements' positions or know the index, so a classic for is still needed for search positions.

A 2D array is an array whose elements are arrays. int[][] grid = new int[3][4] gives three rows of four columns, but int[][] jagged = new int[3][] lets each row have its own length. java.util.Arrays supplies sort, toString, equals, copyOf and binarySearch, which are safer than hand-rolled versions.
hinglish: Array numbered slots ka dabba hai. int[] marks = new int[5] paanch ints banata hai, sab 0 se shuru. Valid index 0 se 4 tak — marks[5] maangoge to ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException aayega, kyunki last index length - 1 hota hai.
2D array asal me array of arrays hai, isliye har row ki length alag ho sakti hai (jagged). java.util.Arrays me sort, toString, equals, copyOf aur binarySearch ready hain — haath se likhne se safer.
modules.analogy: Array ek train ke reserved seats jaisa hai: seats ki ginti fix hai, har seat ka number zero se shuru hota hai, aur aap seedha seat number se pahunchte ho. 2D array ek sleeper coach hai — har bay (row) me alag number of berths ho sakte hain.
modules.why: Arrays are the base of collections, strings, images, matrices and every interview data-structure question. Understanding length, indexing and copies prevents the most common runtime crash in beginner Java code.

syntax.code:
int[] marks = new int[4];        // 0, 0, 0, 0
int[] primes = {2, 3, 5, 7};      // literal
String[] names = new String[2];    // null, null
System.out.println(marks.length); // 4
System.out.println(names[0] == null); // true
syntax.note: length is a field on arrays, not a method. Object arrays default to null; numeric arrays default to 0.
Each row has its own length, so the inner condition uses grid[r].length, not grid[0].length.

topics.title: Declaration and initialisation
topics.body: Type[] name = new Type[size] or a literal {…}. Arrays are objects on the heap; the variable holds a reference. Uninitialised numeric elements are 0, booleans false, references null.

topics.title: Traversal and the length field
topics.body: Indexes run 0..length-1. A for-each loop is cleaner for reading values; a classic for gives you the index. Use array.length (field) for arrays and text.length() (method) for Strings.

topics.title: Searching
topics.body: Linear search checks each element: O(n) and works on unsorted data. Binary search is O(log n) but needs a sorted array; Arrays.binarySearch returns the index or a negative insertion point.

topics.title: Sorting
topics.body: Bubble, selection and insertion sort are O(n²) teaching algorithms. Arrays.sort uses a tuned dual-pivot quicksort for primitives and a stable merge sort for objects, and is what production code should call.

topics.title: 2D and jagged arrays
topics.body: int[][] is an array of int[]. new int[3][4] allocates every row; new int[3][] leaves rows null until you allocate them. Iterate rows, then columns of that row.

topics.title: Copying and Arrays utilities
topics.body: Arrays.copyOf copies with a new length, System.arraycopy copies ranges, and clone makes a shallow copy. Arrays.toString/equals/deepToString/fill/sort/binarySearch/stream cover most day-to-day needs.

topics.title: Debugging array code
topics.body: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException means an index was outside 0..length-1. Print length and the index just before the access. NullPointerException on a 2D row usually means the row was never allocated.

examples.title: Sum, average and maximum
lines: marks is a literal array of five ints; its length is fixed at 5.
max starts at marks[0] so it is valid even for all-negative arrays.
The for-each loop reads each value once, accumulating the sum and tracking the maximum.
Average casts sum to double before dividing, otherwise 396 / 5 would be 79.

examples.title: Jagged rows and row sums
examples.output:
row 0: [1, 2] sum=3
row 1: [3, 4, 5] sum=12
row 2: [6] sum=6
3 rows, last row length 1
lines: The outer loop walks three rows; each row is its own int array.
The inner for-each adds that row's values, whatever the row length is.
Arrays.toString prints the row contents in brackets without a loop of our own.
The last line reads the row count and the final row's length, which is 1 — proof the rows differ.

mistakes.wrong: for (int i = 0; i <= nums.length; i++) sum += nums[i];
mistakes.right: for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) sum += nums[i];
mistakes.why: <= reads one past the last valid index, which throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

mistakes.wrong: int[] copy = nums; copy[0] = 99;
mistakes.right: int[] copy = Arrays.copyOf(nums, nums.length); copy[0] = 99;
mistakes.why: Assignment copies the reference, so both variables point at the same array. Use copyOf or clone for a new array.

debug.brief: This sum loop crashes on the last element. Fix the boundary.
hints: The valid indexes are 0, 1 and 2.
The loop condition must be strictly less than length.

best: Use < length, never <= length.
Prefer for-each for reading, indexed for when the position matters.
Use Arrays.sort instead of writing a sort in production code.
Copy arrays with Arrays.copyOf/clone; assignment only copies the reference.
modules.tip: Interviewers ask linear versus binary search and expect the sorted precondition for binary search. Mention Arrays.binarySearch returns a negative value encoding the insertion point when the key is missing.
revision: Arrays are fixed-size, zero-indexed and use the length field.
Indexes 0..length-1; <= length is the classic crash.
2D arrays are arrays of arrays, so rows can be jagged.
Arrays.sort sorts in place; Arrays.toString prints contents.

practice.title: Reverse an array
practice.prompt: Reverse an int array in place with two pointers and print it.
practice.hint: Swap i and j, moving toward the middle.

practice.title: Second largest
practice.prompt: Find the second largest distinct value in an array in one pass.
practice.hint: Track largest and secondLargest; skip duplicates of largest.

practice.title: Matrix transpose
practice.prompt: Print the transpose of a 3×3 matrix.
practice.hint: Output row r, column c as input[c][r].

mcqs.q: What is the last valid index of int[] a = new int[5]?
mcqs.explain: Indexes run 0..length-1, so the last is 4.

mcqs.q: Which prints an array's contents readably?
mcqs.explain: Arrays.toString formats elements; printing the array directly prints a type@hash code.

mcqs.q: Binary search requires…
mcqs.explain: Binary search halves the range using ordering, so the input must be sorted.

interview.q: Array versus ArrayList?
interview.a: Arrays are fixed-size and can hold primitives; ArrayList is resizable, holds objects only (with autoboxing for primitives) and offers add/remove. Arrays are faster and lighter when the size is known.
interview.followUp: Which is better for frequent insertions in the middle? (Neither is great — a linked list is O(1) at a known node, though arrays still win for most real access patterns.)

interview.q: How do you find the second largest element in one pass?
interview.a: Keep largest and secondLargest. For each value: if it is greater than largest, move largest into secondLargest and set largest; else if it is greater than secondLargest and not equal to largest, update secondLargest. O(n) time, O(1) space.
interview.followUp: What if all elements are equal? (No second largest exists; return a sentinel or throw, and say why.)

lab.title: Array sum and maximum
lab.brief: Read n, then n integers. Print the sum and the maximum on two lines.
hints: Start max at nums[0], not 0 — otherwise all-negative arrays fail.
Use a long sum if n can be large.

checkpoint.title: Arrays indexed correctly?
checks: I never write <= array.length
I can traverse a jagged 2D array without a fixed column count
I copy arrays with Arrays.copyOf instead of assignment

modules.title: Object-Oriented Programming
modules.goal: Class, object, constructor, encapsulation aur object lifecycle par solid foundation.
objectives: Design a class with private fields, a constructor and behaviour
Explain what this refers to and when a constructor runs
Tell static state apart from instance state
Protect invariants with encapsulation and validation
modules.definition: A class is a blueprint: it declares fields (state) and methods (behaviour). An object is an instance of that class created with new. A constructor initialises a new object. Encapsulation keeps fields private and exposes controlled access through methods so the object's invariants stay true.
explain: A class groups the data and the operations that belong together. Each object gets its own copy of the instance fields; methods describe what every instance can do. Creating an object with new runs a constructor, which is where required state is set up.

this is the current object's reference. It disambiguates a field from a parameter with the same name (this.balance = balance), lets one constructor call another (this(0)), and passes the object to another method.

Encapsulation means fields are private and can only change through methods that enforce the rules. A balance cannot go negative if deposit and withdraw are the only ways to change it. Static fields belong to the class — one copy shared by every instance — which is why they are useful for counters but dangerous for mutable shared state.
hinglish: Class blueprint hai, object us blueprint se bana actual instance. Har object ke apne instance fields hote hain, aur methods batate hain ki us object ke saath kya kaam ho sakta hai. new karte hi constructor chalta hai, jahan required state set hoti hai.

this current object ko point karta hai — field aur parameter ka naam same ho to this.balance = balance likhte hain. Encapsulation ka matlab: fields private, aur unhe badalne ka sirf ek controlled raasta. static field class ka hota hai, saare objects ek hi copy share karte hain.
modules.analogy: Class ek car ka design document hai; object us design se bani actual car. Har car ka apna odometer (instance field) hota hai, par factory ka total-produced counter (static field) sab cars ke liye ek hi hota hai.
modules.why: Java is object-oriented at its core, and every framework you will touch — Spring, JPA, JUnit — is built from classes with constructors and injected dependencies. Encapsulation is also what makes code safe to change: callers depend on methods, not on private representation.

syntax.note: Private field, validating constructor, behaviour that enforces the rule, and a getter for reading. No setter for balance: it can only move through deposit/withdraw.
Static members are read through the class name. Instance members are read through a reference.

topics.title: Classes, objects, fields and methods
topics.body: A class declares state and behaviour. new creates an object on the heap and returns a reference. Instance fields hold per-object state; methods read and change it.

topics.title: Constructors
topics.body: A constructor has the class name and no return type. If you write none, Java supplies a no-argument default constructor; once you write one, the default is no longer generated. Constructors can be overloaded and can call each other with this(...).

topics.title: The this keyword
topics.body: this is the current instance. It resolves field/parameter name clashes, chains constructors, and passes the object onward. You cannot use this in a static context, because there is no instance.

topics.title: Static versus instance state
topics.body: Static fields and methods belong to the class and are shared; instance members belong to one object. Static mutable state is global state — convenient for counters, risky for anything else, especially in multithreaded code.

topics.title: Access modifiers and encapsulation
topics.body: private (class only), package-private (same package, the default), protected (package plus subclasses), public (everywhere). Keep fields private; expose the smallest API that callers need.

topics.title: Getters, setters and invariants
topics.body: A getter reads state; a setter should validate before assigning. Prefer behaviour methods (deposit) over raw setters when a rule exists, so the object cannot be put into an invalid state.

topics.title: Object lifecycle
topics.body: An object is created by new, becomes reachable through a reference, and is garbage-collected once nothing reachable points at it. Java has no deterministic destructor; try-with-resources or close() handles external resources.

examples.title: An encapsulated account
lines: balance is private, so no caller can set it directly to an invalid value.
The constructor rejects a negative opening balance.
withdraw(200) returns false and changes nothing, because 200 > 100 + 50.
withdraw(120) succeeds, leaving 30.00, printed with two decimals.

examples.title: Static counter, instance identity
lines: created is static: one counter shared by every Employee.
id is final: it is assigned once in the constructor and never changes.
++created increments first, so the first employee gets id 1.
Employee.created is read through the class name; it is 2 after two objects.

mistakes.wrong: class User { public String name; public int age; }
mistakes.right: class User { private String name; private int age; public String getName() { return name; } }
mistakes.why: Public fields let any caller set invalid values (negative age, null name). Private fields plus validating methods keep the object valid.

mistakes.wrong: void Account(double opening) { balance = opening; }
mistakes.right: Account(double opening) { balance = opening; }
mistakes.why: A return type turns the constructor into an ordinary method, so new Account(100) would use the default constructor and leave balance at 0.

debug.brief: This class is meant to say hello from an object, but main does not compile. Fix the constructor/method call.
hints: greet is an instance method, not static.
Call it on the object you created.

best: Keep fields private and make the class's invariants explicit in its methods.
Validate constructor arguments and fail fast with IllegalArgumentException.
Prefer final fields for values that should not change after construction.
Avoid static mutable state unless it is genuinely class-wide (a counter, a cache with care).
modules.tip: When asked 'what is encapsulation?', do not stop at 'private fields'. Add that the object protects its invariants and that callers depend on behaviour, so the representation can change without breaking them.
revision: Class = blueprint, object = instance, constructor = initialiser.
this refers to the current object and chains constructors.
static = one copy for the class; instance = one per object.
Encapsulation keeps fields private and rules in methods.

practice.title: Rectangle class
practice.prompt: Create Rectangle with private width/height, a validating constructor, area() and perimeter().
practice.hint: Reject non-positive dimensions in the constructor.

practice.title: Bank account
practice.prompt: Add deposit, withdraw and a transaction count kept in a static field.
practice.hint: Increment the static counter inside each successful operation.

practice.title: Student report
practice.prompt: Model Student with name and marks array, plus average() and a grade() method.
practice.hint: Keep the marks array private and copy it in the constructor.

mcqs.q: What does this refer to in an instance method?
mcqs.explain: this is the reference to the object the method was called on.

mcqs.q: When is the default no-argument constructor provided?
options: Only when no constructor is declared
mcqs.explain: Once you declare any constructor, the compiler no longer adds the default one.

mcqs.q: A static field belongs to…
mcqs.explain: Static members are class-level and shared by all instances.

interview.q: What is encapsulation and why does it matter?
interview.a: Encapsulation hides an object's representation behind a controlled API: fields are private and methods enforce the rules. It matters because invalid states become impossible to create, and the internal representation can change without breaking callers.
interview.followUp: Does a getter/setter pair always mean encapsulation? (No — a blind setter exposes state just as much as a public field.)

interview.q: Can a constructor be private?
interview.a: Yes. A private constructor prevents external instantiation, which is how singletons and utility classes work. Static factory methods can still create instances internally.
interview.followUp: How does that interact with inheritance? (A subclass cannot call a private constructor, so the class cannot be subclassed unless it exposes another accessible constructor.)

lab.title: Rectangle with behaviour
lab.brief: Read width and height, then print area and perimeter using a Rectangle class.
hints: area = width * height; perimeter = 2 * (width + height).
Print the doubles directly; Java prints 24.0.

checkpoint.title: Objects modelled properly?
checks: I can write a constructor that validates its arguments
I know when to use this and why static cannot use it
My fields are private and my invariants are enforced in methods

modules.title: Inheritance and Polymorphism
modules.goal: extends, super, method overriding aur runtime polymorphism ka asli behaviour.
objectives: Model an is-a relationship with extends and call the parent constructor with super
Override a method and explain dynamic dispatch
Tell compile-time (overloading) from runtime (overriding) polymorphism
Choose composition when inheritance is the wrong tool
modules.definition: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and specialise a superclass (is-a). Overriding replaces an inherited method with the same signature; the JVM chooses the override at runtime based on the object's actual class (dynamic dispatch). Overloading is a compile-time choice based on argument types.
explain: A subclass inherits accessible fields and methods and can add its own. super(...) calls the parent constructor and must be the first statement; super.method() calls the parent's version. Constructors are not inherited.

When a superclass reference points at a subclass object, the method that runs is the subclass's override. That is dynamic dispatch, decided at runtime from the object, not the variable's type. Fields do not behave this way — field access is resolved from the reference type, which is why overriding methods is safer than hiding fields.

Inheritance is a strong coupling: a subclass depends on the parent's implementation. Use it when the subtype genuinely is a specialised parent; otherwise compose — hold the other object as a field and delegate. final on a class blocks subclassing, and final on a method blocks overriding.
hinglish: Subclass parent ke accessible fields/methods inherit karta hai. super(...) parent constructor call karta hai aur pehla statement hona chahiye. Parent reference agar child object ko point kare, to runtime par child ka override chalta hai — isi ko dynamic dispatch kehte hain.

Inheritance strong coupling hai: child parent ke implementation par depend karta hai. Sirf tab use karo jab sach me is-a relationship ho; warna composition better hai — doosre object ko field ki tarah rakho aur kaam delegate karo. final class ko extend hone se rokta hai.
modules.analogy: Parent class ek generic smartphone hai; subclass ek camera-focused model hai jo sab kuch inherit karta hai aur camera app ko apne tareeke se override karta hai. Aap 'phone' bolkar bhi camera model chala sakte ho — jo actual device hai wahi behaviour chalega.
modules.why: Frameworks are built on polymorphism: Spring injects an interface, tests replace it with a fake, and your code calls the same method either way. Interviewers test the difference between overriding and overloading because it exposes whether you understand compile-time versus runtime binding.

syntax.note: @Override is checked by the compiler: if the signature does not override anything, it fails instead of silently overloading.
super(name) runs the parent constructor; super.pay() reuses the parent calculation instead of duplicating it.

topics.title: Inheritance shapes
topics.body: Single: one parent. Multilevel: A → B → C. Hierarchical: several subclasses share one parent. Java allows only single class inheritance to avoid the diamond ambiguity; interfaces provide the multiple-type behaviour.

topics.title: super
topics.body: super(...) invokes a parent constructor and must be first. super.method() calls the parent implementation. If you do not call super(...), the compiler inserts super() and fails if no no-argument parent constructor exists.

topics.title: Overriding rules
topics.body: Same name, same parameter list, compatible (covariant) return type, and no more restrictive access. private, static and final methods cannot be overridden. Use @Override so the compiler verifies your intent.

topics.title: Runtime polymorphism and dynamic dispatch
topics.body: The JVM selects the override from the object's runtime class. This is what lets a List<Shape> call area() on circles and rectangles without an if-else chain.

topics.title: Compile-time polymorphism
topics.body: Overloading is resolved by the compiler from the declared argument types. It is not dispatch: the choice is fixed in the bytecode.

topics.title: final and the Object class
topics.body: final class cannot be extended; final method cannot be overridden; final field is assigned once. Every class extends Object, which supplies toString, equals, hashCode and getClass — override toString for readable output and equals/hashCode together for value equality.

topics.title: Composition versus inheritance
topics.body: Composition holds another object and delegates. It avoids fragile base classes, keeps APIs small and lets you change behaviour at runtime. Prefer it unless the subtype really is a parent.

examples.title: Dynamic dispatch through a parent reference
lines: Dog and Cat both extend Animal and call super(name) to set the inherited field.
Each subclass overrides speak with its own message.
The array is typed Animal, but each element is a Dog or Cat object.
At runtime the JVM calls the override belonging to the actual object, so two different lines print.

examples.title: super, final and toString
lines: Manager's constructor delegates to Employee's constructor with super(name).
Manager.pay() adds the bonus to super.pay() instead of hardcoding 40,000.
Manager.toString() reuses the parent's formatting with super.toString().
println uses toString(); e.pay() dispatches to Manager.pay() even through an Employee reference.

mistakes.wrong: class Dog extends Animal { void Speak() { } }
mistakes.right: class Dog extends Animal { @Override void speak() { } }
mistakes.why: Java is case-sensitive, so Speak overloads instead of overriding. @Override would have reported the mistake at compile time.

mistakes.wrong: class Manager extends Employee { Manager() { } }
mistakes.right: class Manager extends Employee { Manager() { super(); } }
mistakes.why: If the parent has no no-argument constructor, the implicit super() call cannot compile; you must call the parent constructor explicitly.

debug.brief: This code should print 'Dog barks' but prints the parent message. Find why the override is not used.
hints: Compare the method names character by character.
An override must have exactly the same name and parameters.

best: Always add @Override so a signature typo becomes a compile error.
Keep the parent's contract in mind: an override must not weaken it.
Prefer composition when the relationship is has-a or when you only want to reuse code.
Override toString for readable logs; override equals and hashCode together.
modules.tip: If asked 'what is polymorphism?', give both forms with one line each — overloading resolved at compile time, overriding dispatched at runtime — and add a concrete example of a parent reference calling a child override.
revision: extends inherits accessible members; constructors are not inherited.
super(...) must be the first statement; super.method() reuses parent logic.
Overriding is runtime dispatch; overloading is compile-time selection.
final blocks inheritance/override; composition is usually safer than deep hierarchies.

practice.title: Shape hierarchy
practice.prompt: Create Shape with area(), then Circle and Rectangle. Print areas from a Shape[] without if-else.
practice.hint: Call shape.area() inside the loop; the object decides.

practice.title: Employee payroll
practice.prompt: Employee.pay() returns base; Manager adds a bonus; Intern returns half. Print all from an Employee[].
practice.hint: Use super.pay() in each override.

practice.title: Composition rewrite
practice.prompt: Rewrite a subclass that only wanted to reuse code as a class holding the old object and delegating.
practice.hint: Replace extends with a private field plus forwarding methods.

mcqs.q: Which method is called by Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak();?
mcqs.explain: Dynamic dispatch uses the object's runtime class, which is Dog.

mcqs.q: Overloading is resolved…
mcqs.explain: The compiler picks the overload from the declared argument types.

mcqs.q: What does @Override do?
options: Asks the compiler to verify it overrides a superclass method
mcqs.explain: It is a compile-time check that prevents accidental overloads from looking like overrides.

interview.q: Overloading vs overriding?
interview.a: Overloading: same method name, different parameter lists, in the same class or a subclass, resolved at compile time. Overriding: same signature in a subclass, replaces the parent behaviour, resolved at runtime by dynamic dispatch.
interview.followUp: Can you override a static method? (No. A static method is hidden, not overridden, and the reference type decides which one is called.)

interview.q: Why prefer composition over inheritance?
interview.a: Inheritance couples a subclass to the parent's implementation, so parent changes can break children (the fragile base class problem). Composition exposes only the delegated API, keeps coupling low and allows behaviour to change at runtime.
interview.followUp: When is inheritance right? (When the subtype truly is a specialised parent and the parent was designed for extension.)

lab.title: Polymorphic areas
lab.brief: Read a shape type then its dimensions: 'circle r' or 'rect w h'. Print the area with two decimals.
hints: Circle area = Math.PI * r * r.
Rect area = w * h; mark both methods @Override.

checkpoint.title: Polymorphism understood?
checks: I can explain why the object, not the variable type, chooses an override
I use @Override on every override
I can name a case where composition is the better design

modules.title: Abstraction and Interfaces
modules.goal: Abstract classes, interfaces, default methods aur SOLID ka practical use.
objectives: Choose between an abstract class and an interface with a reason
Implement multiple interfaces in one class
Use default and static interface methods without abusing them
Explain the first SOLID principles with a code example
modules.definition: Abstraction exposes what an object does while hiding how. An abstract class can hold state and partly implemented behaviour but cannot be instantiated. An interface declares a contract; a class can implement many interfaces, and interfaces may provide default and static methods.
explain: An abstract class is a partially built class: it can have fields, constructors and concrete methods, plus abstract methods that subclasses must implement. It expresses a shared identity with shared code. You extend one.

An interface expresses a capability — Comparable, Runnable, List. A class can implement several, which is how Java gets multiple-type behaviour without multiple inheritance. Since Java 8 interfaces can carry default methods (so old implementers do not break) and static helpers.

Program to the interface, not the implementation. A method that takes List<String> works with ArrayList, LinkedList or a test double. That is the dependency-inversion idea behind Spring injection, and it is why interfaces make code testable.
hinglish: Abstract class adhuri class hai: fields, constructor, concrete methods aur kuch abstract methods. Subclass ko extend karte ho — sirf ek. Interface capability batata hai (Runnable, Comparable), aur ek class kai interfaces implement kar sakti hai.

Interface ke against code likho, implementation ke against nahi. Method List<String> le to ArrayList, LinkedList ya test double — sab chalenge. Yahi idea Spring ki dependency injection aur testability ka base hai.
modules.analogy: Interface ek job description hai: 'drive a car' — kis car se, ye implementation decide karti hai. Abstract class ek training program hai jisme kuch modules already complete hote hain aur kuch trainee ko khud karne hote hain.
modules.why: Every serious Java codebase is organised around interfaces: repositories, services, listeners, comparators. Interviews ask abstract class versus interface immediately, and SOLID questions assume you can apply the answer to real code.

syntax.note: An abstract class may mix state, shared behaviour and abstract methods. It cannot be instantiated with new.
Interfaces can have abstract, default and static methods. Fields are implicitly public static final.

topics.title: Abstract classes and methods
topics.body: A class with an abstract method must be abstract; it cannot be instantiated. Subclasses either implement every abstract method or are abstract themselves. Abstract classes are ideal for a template with shared state and partial implementation.

topics.title: Interfaces
topics.body: An interface declares method signatures (and constants). Implementing classes supply the bodies. A reference typed as the interface can point at any implementation, which is the basis of substitutability and mocking.

topics.title: Multiple interface implementation
topics.body: A class can implement several interfaces, so it can be Runnable, Comparable and AutoCloseable at once. If two interfaces provide the same default method, the class must override it and can call InterfaceName.super.method().

topics.title: Default and static methods
topics.body: Default methods let an interface evolve without breaking implementers; they should be small and optional. Static interface methods are utility factories scoped to the interface.

topics.title: Functional interfaces
topics.body: An interface with exactly one abstract method is functional and can be implemented with a lambda: Runnable, Comparator, Predicate, Function. @FunctionalInterface makes the compiler enforce the single-method rule.

topics.title: Interface vs abstract class
topics.body: Use an interface for a capability shared by unrelated types, and for the API boundary. Use an abstract class when implementations share state or substantial code and belong to one family. A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class.

topics.title: Encapsulation, abstraction and SOLID
topics.body: Encapsulation hides data; abstraction hides implementation behind a contract. S: one reason to change. O: extend without editing. L: a subtype must honour the parent's contract. I: small interfaces. D: depend on abstractions, not concretions.

examples.title: Abstract template with shared code
lines: Report owns the title and the render format, which every report shares.
body() is abstract, so each report supplies only its own content.
SalesReport passes its title through super and implements body().
render() calls body() polymorphically, producing the final two lines.

examples.title: Two interfaces, one class
lines: Notebook implements both contracts, so it can be used wherever either type is required.
write appends to the private buffer; read exposes it.
The Readable reference only sees read(), which is enough for printing.
instanceof confirms the object also satisfies Writable at runtime.

mistakes.wrong: abstract class Shape { abstract double area(); }  Shape s = new Shape();
mistakes.right: Shape s = new Circle(2);
mistakes.why: An abstract class cannot be instantiated; the compiler rejects new Shape(). Use a concrete subclass.

mistakes.wrong: interface Repo { void save(); default void saveAll(List<Item> items) { for (Item i : items) save(); } }
mistakes.right: Keep default methods small and optional; put required behaviour in the interface contract.
mistakes.why: Default methods are for compatible evolution. Heavy logic in an interface hides dependencies and is hard to override cleanly.

debug.brief: This class does not compile because it does not honour its interface. Implement the missing method.
hints: A concrete class must implement every abstract interface method.
Add public String greet(String name) and return the text.

best: Program to interfaces in method parameters and fields.
Keep interfaces small and purpose-specific (interface segregation).
Use @FunctionalInterface when the interface is meant for a lambda.
Do not add a default method just to avoid changing implementers — fix the design instead.
modules.tip: The abstract-class-versus-interface answer lands when you add a use case: 'a Payment abstract class for shared amount/validation, a Refundable interface because not every payment is refundable'. That shows the design reasoning interviewers listen for.
revision: Abstract class: shared state/code, one parent, cannot instantiate.
Interface: contract/capability, many implementations, default and static methods.
One abstract method = functional interface = lambda-compatible.
Depend on abstractions (D in SOLID) to keep code testable.

practice.title: Shape interface
practice.prompt: Define Shape with area() and perimeter(); implement Circle and Rectangle; print from a Shape[].
practice.hint: Only the interface type belongs in the loop variable.

practice.title: Functional greeting
practice.prompt: Create a functional interface Formatter with format(String) and implement it twice with lambdas.
practice.hint: Assign a lambda to a Formatter variable, then call format.

practice.title: Refactor to an interface
practice.prompt: Take a service class that news up a repository and refactor it to depend on a Repository interface.
practice.hint: Constructor-inject the interface; pass a fake in a test.

mcqs.q: How many classes can a Java class extend?
mcqs.explain: Java allows single class inheritance; multiple interfaces provide the rest.

mcqs.q: An interface with exactly one abstract method can be…
mcqs.explain: That is a functional interface, the target type for a lambda.

mcqs.q: Which SOLID principle says depend on abstractions?
mcqs.explain: Dependency inversion: high-level modules depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations.

interview.q: Abstract class vs interface — how do you decide?
interview.a: Use an interface for a capability or API boundary shared by unrelated types, and when multiple implementations must be substitutable. Use an abstract class when implementations genuinely share state or a template algorithm. A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class.
interview.followUp: Can an abstract class have no abstract methods? (Yes, but then an interface is usually the clearer design.)

interview.q: What is the Liskov substitution principle?
interview.a: A subtype must be usable wherever the supertype is expected without breaking correctness: it must honour the parent's contract, not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions. A Square that changes Rectangle's setWidth behaviour violates it.
interview.followUp: How do you fix a Liskov violation? (Change the hierarchy — often composition instead of inheritance — rather than adding instanceof checks.)

hints: Use String.format("%s paid %.2f", name, amount).
Assign the right implementation to the Payment variable.

I have implemented two interfaces in one class
I can name all five SOLID principles in one line each

modules.title: Packages and Advanced Java Syntax
modules.goal: Packages, enums, records, sealed types, annotations aur generics ka first look.
objectives: Organise classes into packages and use imports correctly
Model fixed sets with enums and data carriers with records
Restrict a hierarchy with sealed interfaces
Read an annotation and explain what it does at compile or run time
modules.definition: A package is a namespace and directory that groups related classes. Enums model a fixed set of constants. Records are compact immutable data carriers. Sealed types restrict which classes may implement or extend them. Annotations attach metadata that tools and frameworks read.
explain: Packages prevent name collisions and express ownership: com.brocode.shop.model, com.brocode.shop.service. The package statement must match the directory path, and import brings a type into scope without copying it.

An enum is a type with a fixed set of instances — perfect for statuses, roles and directions. A record declares its components once and generates a constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString. Both remove a large class of hand-written bugs.

A sealed interface names its permitted subtypes, so a switch over them can be exhaustive and the compiler knows the complete set. Annotations such as @Override, @FunctionalInterface and @Deprecated are checked by the compiler; framework annotations such as @Entity or @Service are read at runtime.
hinglish: Package namespace aur folder structure hai — com.brocode.shop.model jaise. Isse naam clash nahi hote aur ownership clear hoti hai. Enum fixed set of values ke liye, record immutable data carrier ke liye — dono boilerplate hataate hain.

Sealed interface batata hai kaun kaun implement kar sakta hai, isliye switch exhaustive ho sakta hai. Annotation metadata hai: @Override compiler check karta hai, @Entity jaisi annotations frameworks runtime par padhte hain.
modules.analogy: Package ek building ka floor hai jahan related departments baithte hain; import intercom hai jisse doosre floor se baat karte ho. Record ek pre-printed form hai — fields ek baar bharo, baaki details system bhar deta hai.
modules.why: Real Java projects are organised by package, and records/enums/sealed types are the modern way to model data precisely. Framework annotations are how Spring and JPA find your classes, so reading them is a daily skill.

syntax.note: A record's accessors are name() and price(), not getName(). The compact constructor validates before fields are assigned.
The enum switch expression is exhaustive without a default. A sealed interface limits who may implement it.

topics.title: Packages and imports
topics.body: package declares the namespace and must match the folder path. import brings one type (or a whole package with *) into scope; java.lang is imported automatically. Use fully qualified names when two packages share a class name.

topics.title: Access control across packages
topics.body: private is class-only, package-private (no modifier) is same-package, protected adds subclasses, public is everywhere. A public class must live in a file with the same name.

topics.title: Nested and anonymous classes
topics.body: A static nested class is a namespaced helper. An inner class keeps a link to its outer instance. An anonymous class implements an interface on the spot — still useful when a lambda cannot express state or multiple methods.

topics.title: Enums
topics.body: Enums are classes with a fixed set of instances; they can have fields, constructors and methods. values(), valueOf() and switch make them ideal for statuses. Compare with ==, which is safe for enum constants.

topics.title: Records
topics.body: record Point(int x, int y) generates a canonical constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString. Records are shallowly immutable and cannot extend a class. Add validation in a compact constructor.

topics.title: Sealed classes and interfaces
topics.body: sealed … permits Sub1, Sub2 restricts the hierarchy, which makes exhaustive switches possible and models closed domains such as payment results or shapes.

topics.title: Annotations and documentation
topics.body: @Override, @Deprecated, @SuppressWarnings and @FunctionalInterface are compile-time checks. Framework annotations configure runtime behaviour. Javadoc comments (/** … */) with @param and @return generate API documentation.

examples.title: Record validation and an enum switch
examples.output:
Order[id=A-1, amount=499.0, status=PAID]
packing
rejected: amount
lines: The record declaration generates the constructor and accessors for all three components.
The compact constructor validates amount before the record is created.
toString is generated, so printing the record shows every component.
The switch expression over the enum is exhaustive; the invalid order throws and is caught.

examples.title: Sealed hierarchy and a nested class
lines: The sealed interface permits exactly two record implementations.
circle area uses PI r²; the cast is safe because the hierarchy is closed.
Formatter is a static nested helper class, called through its class name.
Both areas are formatted to two decimals by the nested helper.

mistakes.right: p.x()
mistakes.why: Record accessors are named after the components, without a get prefix.

mistakes.wrong: enum Status { NEW, PAID };  if (status.equals("PAID")) …
mistakes.right: if (status == Status.PAID) …
mistakes.why: Enum constants are objects of the enum type, not Strings. Comparing to a String is always false, and == is the correct, null-safe comparison for enums.

hints: Records generate accessors named after the components.
There is no getX() method on a record.

best: Organise by feature or layer, and keep package names lowercase.
Use records for immutable data transfer; do not add mutable state to them.
Use enums instead of String/int constants for fixed sets.
Seal a hierarchy when the set of subtypes is genuinely closed.
modules.tip: If an interviewer asks 'record vs class', mention the generated members, immutability (shallow), the compact constructor, and that records cannot extend a class — then give a DTO or API-response use case.
revision: Packages are namespaces tied to directories; import brings types into scope.
Enums are fixed instance sets; compare with ==.
Records generate constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, toString.
Sealed types restrict subtypes; annotations add checked metadata.

practice.prompt: Create record Item(String name, int qty, double price) with validation and print its values.
practice.hint: Use a compact constructor to reject negative qty.

practice.title: Enum with fields
practice.prompt: Give enum Priority a level field and a label() method; print labels for all constants.
practice.hint: Enum constructors are implicitly private.

mcqs.q: Which members does a record generate?
mcqs.explain: That is the record contract; accessors are named after the components.

mcqs.q: What does sealed permit?
mcqs.explain: sealed … permits restricts the hierarchy to the named subtypes.

mcqs.q: How should two enum constants be compared?
mcqs.explain: There is exactly one instance per constant, so == is correct and null-safe.

interview.q: When would you use a record instead of a normal class?
interview.a: For immutable data carriers where the state is the whole API: DTOs, API responses, value objects, composite map keys. Records remove boilerplate and make equality and printing correct by default. Use a class when you need mutable state, inheritance from a class, or behaviour that dominates the data.
interview.followUp: Are records deep-immutable? (No — components holding mutable objects are still mutable; copy defensively.)

interview.q: What problem do sealed classes solve?
interview.a: They let a library author declare the complete set of subtypes, so consumers and the compiler can reason exhaustively — switches become checkable and adding a subtype becomes a deliberate, visible change.
interview.followUp: How does that relate to pattern matching? (An exhaustive switch over a sealed hierarchy needs no default branch.)

hints: A switch expression over day can return the enum constant.
Group days with case 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 -> DayType.WEEKDAY.

I can switch over an enum exhaustively
I can explain what sealed permits and why it helps

modules.title: Exception Handling
modules.goal: Checked/unchecked exceptions, try/catch/finally aur custom exceptions ko theek se use karna.
objectives: Tell checked exceptions from unchecked ones and Errors
Write try/catch/finally and explain the execution order
Use throw/throws and custom exceptions for domain failures
Avoid swallowing exceptions or using them for control flow
modules.definition: An exception is an object describing an abnormal event. Checked exceptions must be caught or declared; unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and subclasses) are programming errors the compiler does not force you to handle. Errors indicate serious JVM problems. finally always runs, which makes it the place for cleanup.
explain: When a method cannot complete normally it throws an exception. The JVM unwinds the stack looking for a matching catch. If none is found, the thread terminates and prints a stack trace. Catching lets you recover, translate or add context.

Checked exceptions (IOException, SQLException) represent recoverable external failures, so the compiler requires catch or throws. Unchecked ones (NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException, ArithmeticException) usually mean a bug or invalid input. Do not catch RuntimeException to hide a bug.

finally runs whether the try succeeded, threw or returned. try-with-resources is the modern form for anything closeable: it closes resources automatically, in reverse order, without a finally block. Custom exceptions should carry meaning and context, not just a message.
hinglish: Jab method normally complete nahi ho sakta to exception throw hoti hai. JVM stack unwind karke matching catch dhoondta hai; na mile to thread terminate ho jaata hai. Checked exceptions (IOException) compiler handle karwata hai, unchecked (NullPointerException) bugs batati hain.

finally har haal me chalta hai — success, exception ya return. Closeable resources ke liye try-with-resources better hai: automatic close, reverse order, finally ki zaroorat nahi. Custom exception me context rakho, sirf message nahi.
modules.analogy: Exception handling fire drill jaisa hai: alarm (throw), nearest exit plan (catch), aur drill ke baad sab kuch band karna (finally). Agar koi exit plan nahi mila to building khali hoti hai aur poori report (stack trace) print hoti hai.
modules.why: Production Java fails at the boundaries: files, networks, databases and user input. Well-handled exceptions turn a crash into a clear error; poorly handled ones hide bugs for months. Spring's whole error model is built on exceptions and handlers.

syntax.note: Catch the specific type you can handle. finally runs even when the catch returns.
A checked custom exception extends Exception; the method declares throws, so callers must handle it.

topics.title: What exceptions are and where they come from
topics.body: An exception is an object created at the failure point and thrown up the call stack. The stack trace names the exact line and the chain of calls, which is the first thing to read when debugging.

topics.title: Errors versus exceptions
topics.body: Error (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) signals a JVM-level problem you generally cannot recover from. Exceptions represent conditions a program can detect; handle those, and let Errors surface.

topics.title: Checked versus unchecked
topics.body: Checked: must be caught or declared (IOException, SQLException, custom checked types). Unchecked: RuntimeException subclasses (NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException, ArithmeticException). Use checked exceptions for recoverable external failures, unchecked for programming errors.

topics.title: try, catch, finally
topics.body: One try can have several catches, ordered from specific to general. finally runs on success, failure and return. Never put a return in finally — it overrides earlier returns and hides failures.

topics.title: throw, throws and propagation
topics.body: throw raises an instance; throws declares what a method may raise. If a method cannot handle a checked exception, it declares it and lets the caller decide. Wrapping adds context: throw new ServiceException("loading user " + id, cause).

topics.title: Custom exceptions and best practices
topics.body: Create a domain exception when callers need to distinguish a specific failure. Preserve the cause, use clear messages, and never catch and ignore. Return values or Optional are often better than exceptions for expected outcomes.

examples.title: Catch, finally and a clean message
examples.output:
5
cannot divide by zero
cleanup done
program continues
lines: divide(10, 2) returns 5 and prints it.
divide(5, 0) throws ArithmeticException before the next line runs.
The catch prints a clear message instead of a stack trace.
finally runs before control leaves the try, then the program continues after the block.
dryRun: finally prints cleanup done; next println runs

examples.title: Custom checked exception
lines: InsufficientBalance extends Exception, so it is checked and must be declared.
withdraw declares throws, making the failure part of its contract.
The first call succeeds and prints 60.0.
The second throws the checked exception, caught by the specific catch block.

mistakes.wrong: try { risky(); } catch (Exception e) { }
mistakes.right: try { risky(); } catch (IOException e) { log and handle }
mistakes.why: Catching Exception and doing nothing hides every failure, including bugs. Catch what you can handle and keep the cause.

mistakes.wrong: try { read(); } catch (IOException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e.getMessage()); }
mistakes.right: catch (IOException e) { throw new UncheckedIOException("reading config", e); }
mistakes.why: Dropping the cause loses the stack trace that explains why it failed. Always pass the cause.

debug.brief: This program should print 'bad number' for non-numeric input, but it crashes. Catch the right exception.
hints: What does Integer.parseInt throw for non-numeric text?
It is a NumberFormatException, a RuntimeException.

best: Catch the most specific exception you can actually handle.
Never swallow: log with context or translate with the cause attached.
Use try-with-resources for files, streams and connections.
Do not use exceptions for ordinary control flow; validate first.
modules.tip: A frequent question is 'checked vs unchecked — when do you create which?'. Answer with recoverability: a caller can plausibly recover from a checked failure (retry, ask for another file); an unchecked exception signals a programming error the caller cannot fix.
revision: Checked must be caught/declared; unchecked signal bugs.
finally always runs; try-with-resources closes for you.
throw raises, throws declares, and the cause must be preserved.
Catch specific types; never leave an empty catch block.

practice.title: Safe parse
practice.prompt: Read a string and print its integer value, or 'not a number' on failure.
practice.hint: Catch NumberFormatException around parseInt.

practice.title: Custom age check
practice.prompt: Throw an InvalidAgeException (checked) for age < 0 and handle it in main.
practice.hint: Extend Exception and declare throws.

practice.title: Resource cleanup
practice.prompt: Write a class implementing AutoCloseable and show that try-with-resources closes it even after an exception.
practice.hint: close() prints a line; throw inside try to prove it still runs.

mcqs.q: Which exception is unchecked?
mcqs.explain: NullPointerException extends RuntimeException, so it is unchecked.

mcqs.q: When does finally NOT run?
options: When the JVM exits via System.exit
mcqs.explain: System.exit terminates the JVM before finally blocks complete.

mcqs.q: What does throws declare?
options: That a method may raise a checked exception
That an exception was thrown here
mcqs.explain: throws is part of the method contract; throw actually raises an instance.

interview.q: Difference between throw and throws?
interview.a: throw raises an exception object at a point in the code. throws is a method declaration listing the checked exceptions it may propagate, so callers know what they must handle.
interview.followUp: Can you throw a checked exception without declaring it? (Not out of the method — it must be caught locally or declared.)

interview.q: Why is try-with-resources better than finally?
interview.a: It closes AutoCloseable resources automatically, in reverse order, even when the body throws, and it suppresses secondary close exceptions instead of losing the original. There is no risk of forgetting the null check or the close call.
interview.followUp: What happens if close() throws? (It is attached as a suppressed exception to the primary one.)

lab.brief: Read two integers. Print a / b. If b is zero, print 'cannot divide by zero' instead of crashing.
hints: Wrap the division in try/catch ArithmeticException.
You may also check b == 0 first — say which approach you chose and why.

checkpoint.title: Failures handled, not hidden?
checks: I can classify an exception as checked or unchecked
I know exactly when finally runs
My catch blocks keep the original cause and a useful message

modules.title: Collection Framework
modules.goal: List, Set, Map, Queue aur unke trade-offs ko complexity ke saath samajhna.
objectives: Pick the right collection for a task from its complexity and ordering guarantees
Use List, Set, Map, Deque and PriorityQueue correctly
Iterate safely and avoid ConcurrentModificationException
Sort with Comparable and Comparator
modules.definition: The Collection Framework is a set of interfaces and implementations for groups of objects. Collection extends Iterable; List keeps order and allows duplicates; Set forbids duplicates; Queue/Deque model processing order; Map stores key-value pairs and is not a Collection.
explain: Choose by the question you are answering. Need order and duplicates? List (ArrayList for fast indexing, LinkedList for frequent ends). Need uniqueness? Set (HashSet for speed, LinkedHashSet for insertion order, TreeSet for sorted order). Need lookup by key? Map.

HashMap gives average O(1) get/put using hashCode and equals; a bad hashCode turns it into O(n). TreeMap and TreeSet keep keys sorted in O(log n). ArrayDeque is the modern stack/queue; PriorityQueue always returns the smallest (or comparator-first) element.

Never modify a collection structurally inside a for-each loop — the iterator detects it and throws ConcurrentModificationException. Use iterator.remove(), removeIf, or collect into a new collection. For sorting, Comparable is the natural order and Comparator is an external, composable order.
hinglish: Collection choose karne ka rule sawaal se aata hai: order aur duplicates chahiye to List; uniqueness chahiye to Set; key se lookup chahiye to Map. ArrayList indexing me fast hai, LinkedList ends par fast, HashSet unique + fast, TreeSet sorted.

for-each ke andar collection ko structurally modify karoge to ConcurrentModificationException aata hai. iterator.remove(), removeIf ya nayi list use karo. Comparable natural order hai, Comparator bahar se diya gaya order — dono interview favourites hain.
modules.analogy: List ek queue hai jahan log line me khade hain (duplicates allowed), Set ek guest list hai jahan ek naam ek baar, Map ek dictionary hai jahan word se meaning milti hai, aur PriorityQueue hospital ki triage line hai — sabse urgent pehle.
modules.why: Almost every Java program stores more than one value, and interviews ask ArrayList vs LinkedList, HashMap internals and Comparable vs Comparator. Choosing the wrong collection is a common silent performance bug.

syntax.note: Program to the interface (List, Map) and instantiate the implementation (ArrayList, HashMap). getOrDefault avoids a null check.
Comparator composes: shortest first, then alphabetical. sort mutates the list in place.

topics.title: The hierarchy
topics.body: Iterable → Collection → List, Set, Queue. Map sits beside Collection and maps keys to values. Each interface promises behaviour; the implementation chooses the performance.

topics.title: List: ArrayList and LinkedList
topics.body: ArrayList is a growable array: O(1) random access, O(n) insert/remove in the middle, amortised O(1) append. LinkedList is a doubly linked list: O(1) at both ends, O(n) get(i), more memory per element. Vector is synchronised legacy — prefer ArrayList or CopyOnWriteArrayList.

topics.title: Set: HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet
topics.body: HashSet: average O(1), no order. LinkedHashSet: insertion order, slightly more memory. TreeSet: sorted, O(log n), needs Comparable or a Comparator. Duplicate detection is the point of every Set.

topics.title: Map: HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap
topics.body: HashMap: average O(1), key order unspecified. LinkedHashMap: insertion (or access) order. TreeMap: sorted keys, O(log n). Hashtable is legacy and synchronised; ConcurrentHashMap is the concurrent choice.

topics.title: Queue, Deque and PriorityQueue
topics.body: Queue offers/ polls from the head. ArrayDeque is the preferred stack and queue (push/pop, offer/poll). PriorityQueue returns the least element by natural order or a Comparator, with O(log n) insert and O(log n) poll — not a sorted list.

topics.title: Iteration and fail-fast behaviour
topics.body: for-each uses an Iterator. Structural modification during iteration makes the iterator fail fast with ConcurrentModificationException. Remove through iterator.remove(), removeIf, or build a new collection.

topics.title: Comparable and Comparator
topics.body: Comparable<T>.compareTo defines the natural order inside the class. Comparator<T> defines external orders and composes with comparing, thenComparing, reversed and nullsFirst. Use Comparator for multiple sort orders.

topics.title: Collections utility and complexity
topics.body: Collections.sort, unmodifiableList, singletonList, emptyList, reverse, shuffle, frequency, max/min. Know the table: ArrayList get O(1); HashMap get/put O(1) average; TreeMap O(log n); LinkedList get O(n).

examples.title: Frequency map with deterministic output
lines: TreeMap keeps keys sorted, so the output order is stable without a separate sort.
merge inserts 1 the first time and adds 1 on later occurrences.
entrySet lets us read key and value together without a second lookup.
containsKey checks membership in average O(1) for a hash map and O(log n) here.
dryRun: api and java again → {api=1, java=3, sql=1}

examples.title: Comparable and a composed Comparator
