After Collections.sort, the lowest salary (Aman or Ravi, both 40000) is first — a stable sort keeps Aman before Ravi.
The composed Comparator sorts by salary descending, then by name ascending.
Priya has the highest salary, so she is first after the second sort.
dryRun: Descending salary: Priya 55000, then Aman/Ravi 40000 sorted by name

mistakes.wrong: for (String s : list) { if (s.isEmpty()) list.remove(s); }
mistakes.right: list.removeIf(String::isEmpty);
mistakes.why: Removing through the list during a for-each invalidates the iterator and throws ConcurrentModificationException.

mistakes.wrong: Map<Person, String> map = new HashMap<>(); class Person { }
mistakes.right: Override equals and hashCode consistently on Person.
mistakes.why: HashMap finds a key by hashCode then equals. Without both, equal-looking keys land in different buckets and lookups miss.

debug.brief: This code should remove the empty strings but throws ConcurrentModificationException. Fix it.
hints: The for-each iterator notices that the list changed.
Use removeIf, or iterator.remove().

best: Declare variables as List/Set/Map and construct the implementation at one place.
Use ArrayDeque rather than Stack for new stack code.
Use Map.merge and computeIfAbsent instead of get/null checks.
Return List.copyOf or Collections.unmodifiableList from APIs that must not be mutated.
modules.tip: For 'HashMap internal working', describe buckets by hashCode, collision handling (linked list then tree at 8 entries in one bucket), resize at load factor 0.75, and why equals/hashCode must agree. That level of detail is what is being tested.
revision: List keeps order and duplicates; Set unique; Map key-value; Queue order of processing.
ArrayList O(1) get, LinkedList O(1) ends, HashSet/HashMap O(1) average, TreeSet/TreeMap O(log n).
Never structurally modify during for-each; use removeIf or an iterator.
Comparable = natural order, Comparator = external/composed order.

practice.title: Duplicate finder
practice.prompt: Read n words and print the first word that appears twice, or 'none'.
practice.hint: A HashSet add() returns false when the value already exists.

practice.title: Top scorer
practice.prompt: Store name→marks in a HashMap and print the highest scorer, breaking ties alphabetically.
practice.hint: Stream over entrySet and sort with a composed Comparator.

practice.title: Task queue
practice.prompt: Use a PriorityQueue to process tasks by priority number and print their names in order.
practice.hint: Comparator.comparingInt(Task::priority).

mcqs.q: Which collection keeps insertion order and rejects duplicates?
mcqs.explain: LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order and enforces uniqueness.

mcqs.q: Average complexity of HashMap.get?
mcqs.explain: Hashing gives average constant-time lookup; worst case degrades with collisions.

mcqs.q: Which interface provides compareTo for natural ordering?
mcqs.explain: Comparable is implemented by the class itself; Comparator is external.

interview.q: ArrayList vs LinkedList?
interview.a: ArrayList is an array: O(1) random access, O(n) insert/remove in the middle, better cache locality. LinkedList is a doubly linked list: O(1) at the ends, O(n) access by index, more memory per node. In practice ArrayList wins for most workloads.
interview.followUp: When is LinkedList actually better? (When you repeatedly insert/remove at the head through a ListIterator, or use it as a Deque — though ArrayDeque is usually faster.)

interview.q: How does HashMap work internally?
interview.a: Keys are hashed, spread and mapped to a bucket. Equal hashCodes share a bucket, compared with equals. Buckets start as a linked list and convert to a balanced tree when they grow beyond eight entries (with a sufficiently large table). The table resizes at load factor 0.75. get/put are O(1) average, O(n) worst case.
interview.followUp: What happens if you override equals but not hashCode? (Equal keys can hash differently, so lookups miss and duplicates appear.)

lab.title: Word frequency, sorted
lab.brief: Read n, then n words. Print each distinct word and its count as word=count, sorted alphabetically.
hints: freq.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum) counts in one line.
TreeMap already sorts keys alphabetically.

checkpoint.title: Collections chosen by evidence?
checks: I can pick a collection from its ordering, uniqueness and complexity
I know why ConcurrentModificationException happens and how to avoid it
I can sort the same data two different ways with Comparator

modules.title: Generics and Wrapper Classes
modules.goal: Type-safe generic code, bounds, wildcards aur autoboxing ke traps.
objectives: Write a generic class and a generic method with a bounded type
Use wildcards to accept a family of types without unsafe casts
Explain autoboxing, unboxing and the null trap
Read a type-erasure warning and remove it properly
modules.definition: Generics let a class or method work over a type chosen by the caller while the compiler checks usage. Type parameters are erased at runtime but enforced at compile time. Wrapper classes (Integer, Double, Character, Boolean…) turn primitives into objects so they can live in collections.
explain: Before generics, a List held Object and every read needed a cast that could fail at runtime. With List<String>, the compiler rejects adding an Integer and read results need no cast. The type parameter is a promise the compiler verifies.

Bounds restrict a type parameter: <T extends Comparable<T>> lets the method call compareTo. Wildcards describe a family: ? extends Number accepts List<Integer> and List<Double> for reading; ? super Integer accepts lists you can write Integers into. The get/put rule — extends for reading, super for writing — is the practical version.

Generics are erased at runtime, so you cannot create new T(), check instanceof List<String>, or overload on type parameters. Wrapper classes bridge primitives and objects: autoboxing converts int to Integer automatically, unboxing the reverse. Unboxing a null Integer throws NullPointerException, which is the classic trap.
hinglish: Generics se List<String> likhte ho aur compiler check karta hai — galat type daalne par compile error, runtime ClassCastException nahi. Bound (<T extends Number>) se T ke methods use kar sakte ho. Wildcard family batata hai: extends reading ke liye, super writing ke liye.

Runtime par generics erase ho jaate hain, isliye new T() ya instanceof List<String> nahi kar sakte. Wrapper classes primitives ko objects banati hain taaki collections me aa sakein. null Integer ko unbox karoge to NullPointerException — classic trap.
modules.analogy: Generic class ek labelled container hai: 'Box<String>' par label laga hai, isliye usme sirf String hi jaata hai aur nikalte waqt type pata hota hai. Erasure ka matlab: runtime par label mit jaata hai, par compile time par chipping ho chuki hoti hai.
modules.why: All modern Java APIs are generic: List<T>, Optional<T>, Stream<T>, Map<K,V>. Framework code and interviews expect you to read <T extends Comparable<? super T>> without fear, and the autoboxing null trap causes real production NPEs.

syntax.note: A generic class can declare its own type parameter, and a generic method can add another (<R>). Type inference lets the diamond <> fill in the rest.
? extends Number accepts a list of any Number subtype; reading is safe, writing is not allowed.

topics.title: Generic classes
topics.body: Declare <T> after the class name and use T as a field, parameter and return type. The compiler substitutes the type argument at each use and rejects incompatible operations.

topics.title: Generic methods
topics.body: A method declares its own type parameter before the return type: static <T> T first(List<T> items). Inference usually lets callers omit the explicit type argument.

topics.title: Bounded types
topics.body: <T extends Comparable<T>> or <T extends Number> restricts T and gives access to the bound's methods. Multiple bounds are allowed with &, with a class first: <T extends Number & Comparable<T>>.

topics.title: Wildcards and the PECS rule
topics.body: ? extends T is a producer (read from it), ? super T is a consumer (write to it): Producer Extends, Consumer Super. An unbounded ? means 'some unknown type', so you can only read as Object.

topics.title: Wrapper classes and autoboxing
topics.body: Integer, Long, Double, Character, Boolean and friends wrap primitives. Autoboxing inserts Integer.valueOf; unboxing calls intValue. Integer caches -128..127, so == can be true for small values and false for larger ones — always compare with equals.

topics.title: Type erasure and type safety
topics.body: Generic type arguments disappear at runtime; the compiler inserts casts. That is why new T[], instanceof List<String> and overloads differing only by type argument are illegal. Raw types disable the checks and should be avoided.

topics.title: Generics in collections
topics.body: List<String>, Map<String, List<Integer>> and Set<T> carry the type through method signatures. Prefer these over raw types in every API so callers cannot add the wrong value.

examples.title: A generic pair and a bounded maximum
lines: Pair declares two independent type parameters, so a String and an Integer can travel together.
max requires T to be Comparable, which is what allows compareTo.
max(3, 9) infers T = Integer and compares numerically.
max("apple", "mango") infers T = String and compares alphabetically.

examples.title: Wildcards and the autoboxing trap
examples.output:
6.0
4.0
true
false
true
unboxing null failed
lines: The wildcard accepts a List<Integer> and a List<Double> with one method.
Values are read as Number and converted with doubleValue().
Integers in the -128..127 cache are the same object, so == is true; 1000 is not cached, so == is false although equals is true.
Assigning a null Integer to int unboxes it and throws NullPointerException, caught here.
dryRun: int x = null → NPE → catch prints message

mistakes.wrong: List list = new ArrayList(); list.add("text"); int n = (int) list.get(0);
mistakes.right: List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); String s = list.get(0);
mistakes.why: Raw types disable checking, so the mistake becomes a runtime ClassCastException instead of a compile error.

mistakes.wrong: Integer count = null; if (count > 0) …
mistakes.right: if (count != null && count > 0) …
mistakes.why: The comparison unboxes count, so a null value throws NullPointerException.

debug.brief: This generic method should return the larger of two numbers but does not compile. Fix the bound.
hints: compareTo exists only on Comparable types.
Restrict T with extends Comparable<T>.

best: Use generics everywhere instead of raw types or Object.
Remember PECS: extends for reading, super for writing.
Compare wrappers with equals, never ==.
Prefer primitive types for hot numeric loops; autoboxing allocates.
modules.tip: If asked why Java generics are invariant (List<Integer> is not a List<Number>), explain that allowing it would permit adding a Double to a list of Integers. Then show that ? extends Number permits reading safely.
revision: Generics move type errors from runtime to compile time.
Bounded types expose methods of the bound.
PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.
Autoboxing caches small Integers; == compares references, equals compares values.

practice.title: Generic stack
practice.prompt: Implement a Stack<T> with push, pop and isEmpty using an ArrayList<T>.
practice.hint: pop should throw IllegalStateException when empty.

practice.title: Bounded count
practice.prompt: Write countGreaterThan(List<? extends Comparable<T>>, T) — or a simpler bounded version — and test with Strings.
practice.hint: Read values, compare with compareTo > 0.

practice.title: Sum any numbers
practice.prompt: Write total(List<? extends Number>) and print results for Integer, Double and Long lists.
practice.hint: Accumulate with doubleValue().

mcqs.q: What does <T extends Comparable<T>> allow?
mcqs.explain: The bound restricts T to types implementing Comparable<T> and permits compareTo.

mcqs.q: Which wildcard is for writing into a structure?
mcqs.explain: Consumer Super: ? super T accepts values of type T.

mcqs.q: Why can == fail for Integer values above 127?
mcqs.explain: Only cached values share objects; larger values are distinct objects, so == compares references.

interview.q: What is type erasure and what does it prevent?
interview.a: Generic type arguments are removed at runtime; the compiler inserts casts. It prevents new T(), instanceof List<String>, generic arrays and overloads that differ only by type argument, because those types no longer exist at runtime.
interview.followUp: How do frameworks still know the type? (They capture it in a superclass generic signature or take a Class<T> token.)

interview.q: Why must equals and hashCode be consistent for wrapper keys?
interview.a: HashMap locates a key by hashCode, then confirms with equals. If equal values produce different hashes, the map looks in the wrong bucket and the key appears missing. For wrappers this is already correct; the rule matters for your own key classes.
interview.followUp: What about mutable keys? (Mutating a field used in hashCode makes the entry unreachable — use immutable keys.)

lab.title: Generic maximum
lab.brief: Read n then n integers. Print the largest using a generic <T extends Comparable<T>> max method.
hints: Start with values.get(0) and compare each element with compareTo.
Return the element whose compareTo is greater.

checkpoint.title: Type-safe and box-aware?
checks: I can write a generic method with a bound
I can explain PECS without reciting the acronym only
I know why Integer == can be true at 127 and false at 1000

modules.title: File Handling and Java I/O
modules.goal: Files, streams, readers/writers, NIO aur try-with-resources se safe I/O.
objectives: Read and write text files with the Files API
Choose between byte streams and character streams
Buffer I/O for performance and close resources automatically
Handle missing files and I/O failures without crashing
modules.definition: Java I/O moves bytes through InputStream/OutputStream and characters through Reader/Writer. The NIO.2 Files API wraps paths with convenient static methods (readString, writeString, lines, copy, move, delete) and reports failures as IOException.
explain: A Path locates a file; Files performs operations on it. Files.readString/readAllLines load text, Files.writeString/write create or overwrite, and Files.lines streams a large file line by line without loading it all into memory.

Byte streams handle binary data (images, PDFs); character streams handle text and apply an encoding. Always specify UTF-8 explicitly rather than relying on the platform default, or the same file will read differently on another machine.

Buffering batches small reads and writes into larger ones, which is dramatically faster for many small operations. Resources must be closed; try-with-resources does that for you even when an exception is thrown, and keeps the original exception if close also fails.
hinglish: Path file ka address hai, Files uspar kaam karta hai. readString poori file padhta hai, Files.lines badi file ko line-by-line stream karta hai bina sab memory me load kiye. Text ke liye encoding hamesha UTF-8 likho.

Byte streams binary ke liye, character streams text ke liye. Buffering chhote reads/writes ko batch karke speed badhata hai. Resource close karna zaroori hai — try-with-resources exception ke baad bhi close karta hai.
modules.analogy: File ek almirah hai, Path uski chabi ka label, aur Files API haath. Buffered reader ek trolley hai — ek-ek item le jaane ke bajaye poora rack ek baar me le aata hai.
modules.why: Every backend reads configuration, writes logs, imports CSV and exports reports. Getting encoding, closing and error handling right prevents data corruption and file-handle leaks that only appear under load.

syntax.note: writeString creates or truncates the file. deleteIfExists avoids an exception when the file is already gone.
try-with-resources closes the reader on every path, including an exception.

topics.title: File and Path
topics.body: java.io.File is the legacy abstraction; java.nio.file.Path is the modern one. Path.of, resolve, getParent, toAbsolutePath and Files.exists cover most path work. Paths are immutable values.

topics.title: Reading and writing text
topics.body: Files.readString/readAllLines for small files, Files.writeString/write for output, Files.lines for a lazy stream over a large file. Always pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8.

topics.title: BufferedReader and BufferedWriter
topics.body: Buffering reduces system calls. readLine returns null at end of file; newLine writes the platform line separator. Wrap FileReader/FileWriter or use Files.newBufferedReader/newBufferedWriter.

topics.title: Byte streams
topics.body: InputStream/OutputStream move raw bytes. Use them for images, archives and binary protocols; layer a Reader/Writer with an explicit charset when the bytes are text. Files.newInputStream/newOutputStream are the NIO entry points.

topics.title: NIO.2 utilities
topics.body: Files.copy, move, delete, createDirectories, walk and list make filesystem work short. Files.walk returns a Stream<Path> that must be closed (try-with-resources).

topics.title: Serialization and its limits
topics.body: Java serialization (Serializable, ObjectOutputStream) persists object graphs but is brittle across versions and unsafe for untrusted input. Prefer JSON/CSV for data exchange and a schema you control.

topics.title: Resource management
topics.body: Close streams, readers and channels. try-with-resources closes in reverse order and suppresses secondary exceptions. Never close a stream you did not open (for example System.out).

examples.title: Write, read and count lines
lines: createTempFile gives a unique path so the program never overwrites a real file.
writeString stores the three lines as UTF-8 bytes.
readString returns the text; lines() splits it lazily and count() returns 3.
findFirst returns the first line, and deleteIfExists cleans up even if reading failed.

examples.title: Buffered reading with try-with-resources
lines: The file holds two lines, written with an explicit UTF-8 charset.
newBufferedReader returns a reader that closes with the try block.
readLine returns null at end of file, which ends the loop.
Each line is split on whitespace to count words: 2 + 2 = 4.
dryRun: reader closed; file deleted in finally

mistakes.wrong: FileReader reader = new FileReader("data.txt"); String s = reader.read() + "";
mistakes.right: try (BufferedReader r = Files.newBufferedReader(Path.of("data.txt"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) { … }
mistakes.why: An unclosed reader leaks a file handle, and the platform default charset makes the text machine-dependent.

mistakes.wrong: Files.writeString(path, text); // called inside a loop for every line
mistakes.right: Build the text with StringBuilder and write once, or use BufferedWriter.
mistakes.why: Each write opens and closes the file; batching is dramatically faster.

debug.brief: This program writes a file and then reads it, but prints an empty line because the writer was never closed. Fix it with try-with-resources.
hints: The buffer has not been flushed when the read happens.
Close (or flush) the writer before reading — try-with-resources does it for you.

best: Specify UTF-8 explicitly on every text read and write.
Use try-with-resources for every stream, reader, writer and channel.
Stream large files with Files.lines instead of loading everything.
Never build file paths by string concatenation; use Path.resolve.
modules.tip: A common interview question is 'byte stream vs character stream'. Answer with what they carry, then add that a character stream is a byte stream plus a charset — and that choosing the wrong charset corrupts text without any exception.
revision: Path locates, Files operates; NIO.2 is the modern API.
Byte streams for binary, character streams for text with a charset.
Buffer for performance; close with try-with-resources.
Files.lines streams a file lazily and must be closed.

practice.title: Line counter
practice.prompt: Write a program that writes three lines to a temp file and prints the line count.
practice.hint: Files.writeString then text.lines().count().

practice.title: Copy a file
practice.prompt: Copy a temp file to a second path with Files.copy and verify both exist.
practice.hint: Pass StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING.

practice.title: Word frequency from a file
practice.prompt: Read a temp file line by line and print the most frequent word.
practice.hint: Use a HashMap<String,Integer> with merge.

mcqs.q: Which reads a whole small text file in one call?
mcqs.explain: Files.readString reads all characters into a String with a chosen charset.

mcqs.q: What does BufferedReader.readLine return at end of file?
mcqs.explain: null signals end of stream; an empty line is still a non-null String.

mcqs.q: Why specify UTF-8 explicitly?
options: The platform default varies between machines
mcqs.explain: Without an explicit charset, text is decoded with the machine default and can corrupt.

interview.q: Byte stream vs character stream?
interview.a: InputStream/OutputStream move raw bytes and suit binary data. Reader/Writer move characters and apply a charset, so they suit text. A Reader is essentially a byte stream plus decoding.
interview.followUp: Which would you use for a PDF? (A byte stream — a PDF is binary, not text.)

interview.q: What does try-with-resources guarantee?
interview.a: Every declared resource is closed when the block exits, in reverse declaration order, whether it completed normally or threw. Close failures become suppressed exceptions on the primary failure, so the original cause is not lost.
interview.followUp: What must a resource implement? (AutoCloseable.)

lab.title: Save the lines
lab.brief: Read n, then n lines from input. Write them to a temp file, read the file back, and print 'saved N lines'.
hints: Files.write(path, lines, StandardCharsets.UTF_8).
Count with Files.readAllLines(file).size().

checkpoint.title: Files handled safely?
checks: I use Path/Files rather than raw File where possible
I always specify UTF-8 and close resources
I can explain byte versus character streams

modules.title: Functional Java
modules.goal: Lambdas, functional interfaces, Streams aur Optional se data pipelines banana.
objectives: Write lambdas against the right functional interface
Build a stream pipeline with intermediate and terminal operations
Use collect, reduce and Optional without null checks everywhere
Explain when a parallel stream helps and when it hurts
modules.definition: A lambda is an anonymous function assigned to a functional interface. The Stream API processes a sequence declaratively: intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted) are lazy and return a new stream, and a terminal operation (collect, forEach, reduce, count) triggers the work exactly once.
explain: A functional interface has one abstract method, so the compiler can infer the lambda's shape: Predicate<T> is T → boolean, Function<T,R> is T → R, Consumer<T> is T → void, Supplier<T> is () → T. Method references (String::length) are shorthand when an existing method already fits.

Streams are lazy: filter and map describe work, but nothing runs until a terminal operation asks for a result. That lets the implementation fuse steps and stop early with findFirst. A stream can be consumed once; reusing it throws IllegalStateException.

collect(Collectors.toList()), groupingBy and joining turn streams back into collections and strings. Optional models a value that may be absent, forcing you to handle the empty case instead of risking a NullPointerException. Parallel streams split work across threads but only pay off for large, CPU-bound, easily splittable work — and they must not touch shared mutable state.
hinglish: Functional interface me ek abstract method hota hai, isliye lambda ka shape compiler infer kar leta hai: Predicate T→boolean, Function T→R, Consumer T→void, Supplier ()→T. Method reference tab use karo jab koi existing method exactly fit ho.

Stream lazy hai: filter/map sirf describe karte hain, kaam tab hota hai jab terminal operation aata hai. Ek stream sirf ek baar consume hoti hai — dobara use karoge to IllegalStateException. Optional absent value ko represent karta hai, taaki null checks ki jagah explicit handling ho.
modules.analogy: Stream ek assembly line hai: filter ek quality-check station, map ek transformation station, aur collect truck hai jo end par maal uthata hai. Jab tak truck nahi aata, line start hi nahi hoti — isliye laziness se kaam bachta hai.
modules.why: Modern Java codebases read like stream pipelines, and interviews test whether you know laziness, collectors and Optional. Writing a loop is fine, but knowing when a pipeline is clearer and safer is a senior-level signal.

syntax.note: Each step returns a new stream; collect is the terminal operation that runs the pipeline.
findFirst returns Optional. orElse gives a fallback; map transforms only when a value is present.

topics.title: Lambdas and functional interfaces
topics.body: A lambda is (params) -> expression or a block. It implements a functional interface. @FunctionalInterface documents and enforces the single-method rule. Lambdas capture effectively final locals only.

topics.title: The four core interfaces
topics.body: Predicate<T> (test), Function<T,R> (apply), Consumer<T> (accept), Supplier<T> (get). BiFunction, UnaryOperator, BiConsumer and primitive specialisations (IntPredicate, ToIntFunction) avoid boxing in hot code.

topics.title: Method references
topics.body: Four forms: Type::staticMethod, instance::method, Type::instanceMethod (on a parameter) and Type::new. Use one when the lambda would only forward its argument.

topics.title: Stream sources and intermediate operations
topics.body: Sources: collection.stream(), Arrays.stream, Stream.of, Files.lines, IntStream.range. Intermediate: filter, map, flatMap, distinct, sorted, limit, skip, peek. They are lazy and may be reordered by the implementation.

topics.title: Terminal operations and collecting
topics.body: Terminal: forEach, count, anyMatch/allMatch/noneMatch, findFirst, reduce, collect, toList. Collectors.toList/toSet/toMap, joining, groupingBy, partitioningBy, counting, summingInt cover most reporting needs.

topics.title: Optional
topics.body: Optional<T> is a container that may be empty. Use map/flatMap/filter/orElse/orElseGet/orElseThrow/ifPresent. Do not use it for fields or method parameters in most designs, and never call get() without checking.

topics.title: Parallel streams and performance
topics.body: parallelStream splits work with the common ForkJoinPool. It helps for large CPU-bound independent work and hurts for small data, I/O, ordered output or shared mutable state. Measure before claiming a speedup.

examples.title: Filter, map, sort and collect
lines: filter keeps names starting with A: Aman and Anita.
map converts each to upper case and sorted orders them alphabetically.
mapToInt avoids boxing and summaryStatistics reports the maximum length (Priya, 5).
groupingBy counts names by their first character, giving A=2, P=1, R=1.
dryRun: Priya filtered out; Ravi filtered out; Anita → ANITA
Max length = 5; grouping counts by first letter

examples.title: Optional, map and reduce
lines: parse returns Optional.empty for invalid text instead of throwing to the caller.
flatMap(Optional::stream) drops the empty optionals and keeps the numbers.
reduce sums 4 + 6 = 10.
orElse supplies -1 for the invalid value, and map doubles the present 7 to 14.

mistakes.wrong: Stream<String> s = list.stream(); s.count(); s.forEach(System.out::println);
mistakes.right: Use each stream once; recreate it with list.stream() for a second pass.
mistakes.why: A stream is consumed by its terminal operation; reusing it throws IllegalStateException.

mistakes.wrong: list.stream().forEach(x -> total += x);
mistakes.right: int total = list.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();
mistakes.why: A lambda may not modify a local variable, and shared mutable state breaks under parallel streams. Use reduce or a collector.

debug.brief: This pipeline is meant to print the count of even numbers, but throws IllegalStateException. Fix the reuse.
hints: count() is a terminal operation and consumes the stream.
Create the pipeline twice, or collect it once and reuse the list.

best: Keep pipelines short; extract a named method when a step needs a comment.
Prefer mapToInt/mapToDouble for numeric work to avoid boxing.
Return Optional from search methods, not null.
Measure before parallelising; shared mutable state makes it wrong, not just slow.
modules.tip: When asked 'why are streams lazy?', connect it to short-circuiting: findFirst on an infinite stream can finish because intermediate steps only run when the terminal asks. Then mention that a stream is single-use.
revision: Lambda implements a functional interface; method reference is shorthand.
Intermediate operations are lazy; a terminal operation runs the pipeline.
collect/Collectors turn results back into collections and strings.
Optional models absence; parallel only for large independent CPU work.

practice.title: Long names
practice.prompt: From a list of names, print the upper-cased names longer than 4 characters, sorted.
practice.hint: filter → map → sorted → toList.

practice.title: Group by length
practice.prompt: Group words by their length and print each length with its words.
practice.hint: Collectors.groupingBy(String::length).

practice.title: Optional chain
practice.prompt: Write findUser(id) returning Optional<String>, then print the upper-cased name or 'unknown'.
practice.hint: map(String::toUpperCase).orElse("unknown").

mcqs.q: Which is a terminal operation?
mcqs.explain: collect consumes the stream and produces a result; the others are lazy intermediate steps.

mcqs.q: Predicate<T> represents…
mcqs.explain: test(T) returns a boolean, which is why filter takes a Predicate.

mcqs.q: What happens when you reuse a consumed stream?
mcqs.explain: Streams are single-use; the second terminal operation throws IllegalStateException.

interview.q: Stream vs for loop — when do you use which?
interview.a: Streams read better for filter/map/group pipelines and are easy to parallelise, but have overhead and can obscure index-dependent or stateful logic. A loop is clearer for early exits with complex control flow or for hot inner loops. Choose the readable one and measure if performance matters.
interview.followUp: Are streams always slower? (Not necessarily; for large data the difference is small, and parallel streams can win — measure.)

interview.q: What is Optional for, and what is it not for?
interview.a: Optional is a return type that makes absence explicit and composable. It is not a general null replacement: avoid it for fields, method parameters and collections, and never call get() without a presence check.
interview.followUp: Optional.of vs ofNullable? (of throws on null; ofNullable returns empty.)

lab.title: Sum of squares of evens
lab.brief: Read n then n integers. Print the sum of the squares of the even numbers, using a stream.
hints: filter(n -> n % 2 == 0).mapToInt(n -> n * n).sum().
mapToInt avoids boxing and gives sum() directly.

checkpoint.title: Pipelines readable and correct?
checks: I can name the four core functional interfaces and their shapes
I know which operations are lazy and which run the pipeline
I never reuse a stream or mutate shared state in a lambda

modules.title: Multithreading and Concurrency
modules.goal: Threads, race conditions, synchronization, executors aur CompletableFuture.
objectives: Create threads with Runnable and run work on an ExecutorService
Explain a race condition and fix it with the right primitive
Use CompletableFuture to compose asynchronous steps
Recognise deadlock and avoid shared mutable state
modules.definition: A thread is an independent path of execution inside one process, sharing that process's heap. Concurrency is managing multiple threads safely: without coordination, interleaved reads and writes cause race conditions. Java provides synchronized, volatile, atomics, locks, concurrent collections and executors for this.
explain: Every Java program starts with the main thread. You create another by implementing Runnable and passing it to a Thread, but production code submits tasks to an ExecutorService so threads are pooled and reused instead of created per request.

A race condition happens when two threads read-modify-write the same variable and the interleaving loses an update. count++ is three steps, not one. synchronized makes a block atomic and establishes visibility; AtomicInteger uses a compare-and-set loop; volatile only guarantees visibility, not atomicity of compound actions.

Deadlock happens when threads wait on locks in opposite orders forever. Prevent it by locking in one global order, keeping critical sections small, using timeouts (tryLock) and avoiding nested locks. CompletableFuture composes asynchronous work without blocking a thread on every step; virtual threads (Java 21) make blocking code cheap, but they are an implementation option, not a replacement for understanding shared state.
hinglish: Program main thread se shuru hota hai. Naya kaam Thread + Runnable se ho sakta hai, par production me ExecutorService use karte hain taaki threads pool se reuse hon. count++ teen steps hai, isliye do threads beech me ghus kar update kho sakte hain — yahi race condition hai.

synchronized block ko atomic banata hai aur visibility deta hai; AtomicInteger compare-and-set use karta hai; volatile sirf visibility deta hai, compound action atomic nahi karta. Deadlock tab hota hai jab threads ulte order me locks maangte hain — lock order fix karo, critical section chhota rakho.
modules.analogy: Ek process ek kitchen hai aur threads usme kaam karne wale cooks. Shared counter fridge par laga board hai: do cooks ek saath padhein, dono +1 likhein, to ek update kho jaata hai. synchronized ka matlab hai board par ek waqt me ek hi cook likhega.
modules.why: Servers handle many requests at once, and concurrency bugs are the hardest to reproduce. Interviews ask about thread lifecycle, synchronized vs volatile, executors and CompletableFuture because those are the tools every Java backend uses daily.

syntax.note: start() creates the new path of execution; run() would run it on the current thread. join() makes the caller wait.
submit returns a Future for the result; always shut the pool down or the JVM may keep running.

topics.title: Process vs thread
topics.body: A process has its own memory; threads share the process heap but have their own stack and program counter. Sharing makes communication cheap and race conditions possible.

topics.title: Thread lifecycle and creation
topics.body: NEW → RUNNABLE → (BLOCKED/WAITING/TIMED_WAITING) → TERMINATED. Create with Runnable (preferred) or by extending Thread. start() schedules; run() is just a method call.

topics.title: ExecutorService and thread pools
topics.body: Pools bound the number of threads and reuse them. submit returns Future; invokeAll runs a batch. shutdown lets queued work finish, shutdownNow interrupts. Never create a thread per request in a server.

topics.title: Synchronization and race conditions
topics.body: synchronized(lock) makes a block mutually exclusive and publishes writes. Use one lock object consistently. Keep the critical section small; never call unknown code (or I/O) while holding a lock.

topics.title: volatile, atomics and locks
topics.body: volatile guarantees visibility of a single variable but not atomicity. AtomicInteger/AtomicLong/LongAdder handle counters lock-free. ReentrantLock adds tryLock timeouts and fairness. Prefer the simplest tool that is correct.

topics.title: wait/notify and concurrent collections
topics.body: wait/notify coordinate on an object's monitor but are easy to misuse; prefer BlockingQueue for producer-consumer. ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList and BlockingQueue are the thread-safe collections.

topics.title: CompletableFuture and deadlock
topics.body: CompletableFuture composes async steps with thenApply/thenCompose/thenCombine and handles errors with exceptionally. Deadlock: two threads hold one lock each and wait for the other — fix the lock order or use timeouts.

topics.title: Virtual threads (Java 21)
topics.body: Virtual threads are lightweight threads scheduled by the JVM, so blocking code can scale to many tasks. They reduce the cost of thread-per-task designs; they do not make shared mutable state safe.

examples.title: Two threads, one safe counter
lines: Both threads share one Counter object, so they share the counter state.
increment is synchronized, so the read-modify-write cannot interleave.
join makes main wait for both workers before reading the total.
1000 + 1000 increments are all counted: 2000.
dryRun: thread a and b each loop 1000 times
each increment is atomic under the monitor

examples.title: ExecutorService and futures
lines: A fixed pool of two threads runs three tasks, reusing threads.
invokeAll submits every callable and returns futures in the same order.
get() blocks until that task's result is available.
2+3=5, 4*5=20, 9-1=8, total 33; shutdown releases the pool.

mistakes.wrong: private int count; void inc() { count++; }
mistakes.right: private final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(); void inc() { count.incrementAndGet(); }
mistakes.why: count++ is not atomic; two threads can read the same value and lose an update. Use atomics or synchronize the whole operation.

mistakes.wrong: synchronized (a) { synchronized (b) { … } }  // other thread locks b then a
mistakes.right: Always acquire locks in the same global order, or use one lock.
mistakes.why: Opposite lock orders are the classic deadlock recipe.

debug.brief: This program throws IllegalThreadStateException because it starts the same thread twice. Fix it.
hints: A Thread can be started only once.
Create a new thread for the second run, or start it once.

best: Prefer executors and concurrent collections over raw threads and wait/notify.
Keep shared mutable state minimal; immutable objects need no locks.
Never call blocking I/O or unknown code while holding a lock.
Use timeouts and a consistent lock order to make deadlock unlikely and detectable.
modules.tip: For 'synchronized vs volatile', say synchronized gives mutual exclusion plus visibility, volatile gives visibility only. Then give the counter example: volatile count++ is still broken.
revision: Threads share the heap; each has its own stack.
Race condition = interleaved read-modify-write; fix with synchronization or atomics.
Executors pool threads; Futures return results.
CompletableFuture composes async steps; virtual threads make blocking cheap.

practice.hint: Join every thread before reading the value.

practice.hint: put/take block automatically.

mcqs.q: What does synchronized guarantee?
mcqs.explain: Only one thread executes the block at a time, and writes are visible to the next holder.

mcqs.q: Which is safe for a shared counter?
mcqs.explain: AtomicInteger performs the increment as one atomic operation.

mcqs.q: What causes deadlock?
options: Threads waiting on locks held by each other in a cycle
mcqs.explain: A circular wait on locks is the classic cause.

interview.q: volatile vs synchronized?
interview.a: volatile makes reads and writes of one variable visible across threads and prevents reordering, but a compound action like count++ is still unsafe. synchronized provides mutual exclusion plus visibility, so it protects multi-step invariants.
interview.followUp: When is volatile enough? (A single-writer status flag or a reference published once, where no compound update is needed.)

interview.q: How would you prevent deadlock?
interview.a: Acquire locks in a global order, avoid nested locks, keep critical sections small, use tryLock with a timeout, and prefer lock-free structures or a single lock when contention is low.
interview.followUp: Can you recover from a deadlock? (Not reliably; you can detect it with thread dumps and restart, which is why prevention matters.)

Join both threads before printing.

modules.title: Database and Backend Development
modules.goal: JDBC, SQL integration, Maven/Gradle, REST concepts aur Spring Boot ka mental model.
objectives: Describe the JDBC call flow and why PreparedStatement prevents injection
Model CRUD and a transaction with commit and rollback
Explain Maven/Gradle, HTTP verbs and JSON in a Java backend
Explain dependency injection and what Spring Boot adds
modules.definition: JDBC is the standard Java API for relational databases: a driver implements Connection, PreparedStatement and ResultSet. Backend services expose HTTP endpoints, validate input, call a repository, and return JSON. Spring Boot wires these layers together with dependency injection and auto-configuration.
explain: JDBC follows a fixed flow: load a driver (automatic since JDBC 4), open a Connection, prepare a statement, execute, read the ResultSet, close everything. A PreparedStatement sends SQL and values separately, so user input can never change the query structure — that is the defence against SQL injection.

A transaction groups statements so they all commit or all roll back. Set autoCommit(false), do the work, commit() on success, rollback() in the catch, and always close resources. Isolation levels control which concurrent anomalies are visible; most services start with READ_COMMITTED.

A backend is layered: controller (HTTP), service (rules, transactions), repository (SQL), domain (records/entities). Maven or Gradle resolves dependencies and builds the jar. Spring Boot adds an embedded server, dependency injection and starters, but the layers and the SQL still decide correctness.
hinglish: JDBC ka flow fix hai: Connection kholo, PreparedStatement banao, execute karo, ResultSet padho, sab close karo. PreparedStatement SQL aur values alag bhejta hai, isliye user input query ka structure nahi badal sakta — SQL injection ka asli defence yahi hai.

Transaction me sab statements ek saath commit ya rollback hote hain: autoCommit(false), kaam, success par commit, catch me rollback. Backend layers: controller → service → repository → database. Spring Boot wiring aur server deta hai, par SQL aur rules aap hi likhte ho.
modules.analogy: JDBC ek courier service jaisa hai: Connection phone line hai, PreparedStatement sealed envelope hai jisme address aur content alag hote hain, ResultSet delivery hai. Transaction ek 'all or nothing' parcel hai — kuch bhi fail hua to poora wapas.
modules.why: Most Java jobs are backend jobs: REST APIs over a relational database. Interviewers expect the JDBC flow, PreparedStatement versus Statement, transaction boundaries, and how Spring's dependency injection fits the layers you already know.

syntax.note: Requires a JDBC driver on the classpath. Placeholders are bound with setX, never concatenated.
Both statements succeed together or neither does. The catch preserves the original failure.

topics.title: JDBC architecture and drivers
topics.body: The app talks to java.sql interfaces; the vendor driver implements them. DriverManager.getConnection uses a JDBC URL. Drivers are loaded automatically via the service loader when they are on the classpath.

topics.title: Connection, Statement and PreparedStatement
topics.body: Statement concatenates SQL — unsafe and slower to reuse. PreparedStatement uses ? placeholders, binds typed values, is precompiled/cached and blocks injection. Always prefer it.

topics.title: ResultSet and CRUD
topics.body: executeQuery returns rows; rs.next() advances and returns false at the end. Read columns by name. executeUpdate returns affected rows for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. Map rows to records or entities.

topics.title: Transactions and isolation
topics.body: autoCommit(false), commit/rollback, and a finally that restores the flag. Isolation levels trade consistency for concurrency: READ_COMMITTED avoids dirty reads; SERIALIZABLE is strict and slower.

topics.title: Maven and Gradle
topics.body: Maven uses pom.xml with a fixed lifecycle; Gradle uses build.gradle with a flexible task graph. Both resolve dependencies, compile, test and package. Pin versions, keep the build reproducible, and never commit credentials.

topics.title: REST, HTTP and JSON
topics.body: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates, DELETE removes. Status codes carry meaning: 200/201, 400 validation, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 missing, 409 conflict, 500 server error. JSON is the usual body format; validate and serialise with a library, never string concatenation.

topics.title: Spring Boot, DI and JPA
topics.body: Dependency injection supplies collaborators through constructors instead of new-ing them, which makes testing and configuration possible. Spring Boot auto-configures an embedded server, a DataSource and JSON support from starters. JPA/Hibernate maps entities to tables and manages transactions; JDBC remains the layer underneath.

topics.title: Backend architecture
topics.body: Controller → service → repository, with DTOs at the boundary and domain objects inside. Keep SQL in repositories, transactions in services, and HTTP concerns in controllers. Log with correlation ids; never leak stack traces to clients.

examples.title: Repository CRUD without a database
lines: The repository hides the Map, exactly as a JDBC repository hides SQL.
find returns Optional, so a missing row is explicit rather than null.
delete returns whether a row was actually removed; 9 is absent, so false.
all returns a copy, so callers cannot mutate the repository's internals.

examples.title: Transaction semantics, simulated
lines: The first transfer debits A and credits B, then commits.
The second debits A and then simulates a failure before crediting B.
The catch restores both balances, which is what rollback does in a database.
The final map shows only the committed transfer: A=70, B=30.

mistakes.wrong: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"
mistakes.right: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?" with ps.setString(1, name)
mistakes.why: Concatenation lets input such as ' OR '1'='1 change the query. A placeholder keeps SQL and data separate.

mistakes.wrong: Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(url); … // never closed
mistakes.right: try (Connection c = …; PreparedStatement ps = …) { … }
mistakes.why: Leaked connections exhaust the pool and take the service down under load.

debug.brief: This query builder is vulnerable to injection. Reject dangerous input and print 'blocked'.
hints: A value containing a quote cannot be trusted in a concatenated query.
In real JDBC, use a ? placeholder — here, reject the input to show the check.

best: Use PreparedStatement for every value; never build SQL by concatenation.
Keep transactions short and put the boundary in the service layer.
Close connections, statements and result sets with try-with-resources.
Return DTOs, not entities, from controllers; validate input at the boundary.
modules.tip: When asked 'how does Spring Boot help?', do not list annotations. Describe what it removes: manual wiring (DI), manual server setup (embedded Tomcat), manual DataSource/JSON configuration (starters), while you still own the SQL, transactions and validation.
revision: JDBC flow: Connection → PreparedStatement → ResultSet → close.
PreparedStatement binds values and prevents injection.
Transactions: autoCommit(false), commit on success, rollback on failure.
REST: verbs + status codes + JSON; Spring Boot wires layers with DI.

practice.title: Repository interface
practice.prompt: Write StudentRepository with save/findAll/findById/delete over a Map, then swap the implementation without touching the caller.
practice.hint: Program to the interface; inject it into a service.

practice.title: HTTP status map
practice.prompt: Given an outcome string (created, invalid, missing, error), print the matching HTTP status code.

practice.title: Transaction drill
practice.prompt: Simulate a transfer that fails after the debit and prove both balances are restored.
practice.hint: Capture before-values and restore them in catch.

mcqs.q: Which prevents SQL injection?
mcqs.explain: Placeholders send SQL and data separately, so input cannot change the query structure.

mcqs.q: Which HTTP method usually creates a resource?
mcqs.explain: POST creates; GET reads; PUT replaces; DELETE removes.

mcqs.q: What does rollback do?
options: Undoes uncommitted work in the transaction
mcqs.explain: Rollback discards changes made since the transaction began.

interview.q: Statement vs PreparedStatement?
interview.a: Statement builds SQL as a string, so input can alter the query and every execution re-parses. PreparedStatement uses placeholders, binds typed values, is typically cached and prevents injection. Use it for any value that comes from outside the program.
interview.followUp: Are PreparedStatements always faster? (Often, because of caching, but the security property is the reason to always use them.)

interview.q: What is dependency injection and why does it matter?
interview.a: A class receives its collaborators through its constructor or a container instead of creating them itself. That decouples it from concrete implementations, makes configuration central, and lets tests pass fakes without a database.
interview.followUp: Constructor vs field injection? (Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit and supports immutability; field injection hides them and needs reflection in tests.)

hints: TreeMap keeps ids sorted automatically.
Print the size first, then each entry.

I can explain why PreparedStatement is mandatory for user input

modules.title: Professional Java and Career Preparation
modules.goal: JVM internals, design patterns, clean code, testing aur interview readiness.
objectives: Explain stack, heap, garbage collection and class loading at a working level
Apply singleton, factory, builder and strategy where they fit
Write a unit-testable class and describe how JUnit and Mockito are used
Prepare a structured answer for a Java developer interview
modules.definition: Professional Java is the discipline around the language: understanding how the JVM manages memory, choosing patterns that reduce coupling, writing clean testable code, and using the build, test and version-control tools a team shares.
explain: The JVM stores each thread's call frames on its stack and objects on the heap. The garbage collector reclaims objects that are no longer reachable; you influence it by allocating less and releasing references, not by calling System.gc(). Class loading happens once per class loader: load, link, initialise.

Design patterns are named solutions to recurring design problems. Singleton gives one instance, Factory hides construction, Builder tames many constructor parameters, Strategy swaps an algorithm behind an interface. Used deliberately they reduce coupling; used everywhere they add indirection.

Clean code and tests are what make a codebase maintainable: small methods with intention-revealing names, no duplicated rules, dependencies injected so a test can substitute them. JUnit runs @Test methods with assertions; Mockito supplies controlled fake collaborators. Git records why a change happened, not just what changed.
hinglish: JVM har thread ke call frames stack par aur objects heap par rakhta hai. GC un objects ko hataata hai jinka koi reachable reference nahi bacha — aap allocation kam karke aur references chhod kar madad karte ho, System.gc() se nahi. Class loading load → link → initialise ek baar hoti hai.

Design patterns recurring problems ke named solutions hain: Singleton, Factory, Builder, Strategy. Soch-samajh kar use karo, warna indirection badh jaata hai. Clean code + tests maintainability dete hain: chhote methods, clear names, injected dependencies, JUnit assertions aur Mockito fakes.
modules.analogy: JVM ek factory hai: stack har worker ka kaam ka tray hai, heap central store hai, aur GC wo saaman hataata hai jise koi worker use nahi kar raha. Design patterns factory ke standard procedures hain — har kaam ke liye ek proven tarika.
modules.why: Interviews for Java roles test JVM memory, GC, patterns and testing because those decide whether code survives production. The capstone and your GitHub projects are the evidence recruiters actually read.

syntax.note: A private constructor plus a static instance is the simplest thread-safe singleton. A builder keeps construction readable when there are many optional values.
Strategy: the algorithm is a parameter, so new rules do not edit checkout(). Lambdas make small strategies concise.

topics.title: JVM internals: stack, heap and GC
topics.body: Each thread has a stack of frames; objects and arrays live on the shared heap. Young generation collects short-lived objects cheaply; old generation holds survivors. G1 is the default collector on modern JDKs. Memory leaks in Java are unintended strong references, not forgotten frees.

topics.title: Class loading and JIT
topics.body: Classes are loaded by bootstrap, platform and application class loaders, then linked (verify, prepare, resolve) and initialised. The JIT compiles hot bytecode to native code; that is why a warmed-up JVM is faster than its first run.

topics.title: Performance and memory leaks
topics.body: Measure with a profiler before optimising. Common leaks: static collections that grow forever, listeners never removed, ThreadLocals in pooled threads, caches without eviction. Prefer bounded caches and explicit lifecycle.

topics.title: Design patterns
topics.body: Creational: singleton, factory, builder. Structural: adapter, decorator, facade. Behavioural: strategy, observer, template method. Know one real use for each rather than reciting definitions.

topics.title: SOLID and clean code
topics.body: Small classes with one reason to change, extension without modification, substitutable subtypes, small interfaces, dependencies on abstractions. Names should say intent; comments should explain why, not what.

topics.title: Unit testing with JUnit and Mockito
topics.body: JUnit 5 runs @Test methods; assertEquals/assertThrows express the expectation. Mockito creates fakes and verifies interactions. Test behaviour through public APIs and keep tests fast and independent.

topics.title: Git, debugging and architecture
topics.body: Commit small, explain why, review diffs. Debug with breakpoints, watches and conditional breakpoints before adding prints. Architecture is layering plus dependency direction: HTTP at the edge, rules in services, persistence in repositories.

topics.title: Interview preparation and the capstone
topics.body: Prepare a two-minute project story: problem, design, trade-off, result. Revise collections complexity, equals/hashCode, exceptions, threads and SQL. The capstone must run, have a README and tests, and you must be able to defend every choice.

examples.title: Singleton and Builder together
lines: Config holds one static instance and a private constructor, so nobody can create a second.
Two get() calls return the same reference, which is what == confirms.
The builder starts with a required name and defaults city to unknown.
build() creates an immutable record, printed with its generated toString.
dryRun: Config.get() called twice → same INSTANCE → true

examples.title: Strategy with lambdas, and a real assertion
lines: checkout takes a discount function instead of hardcoding rules.
The 10% strategy returns 900.0.
The flat-100 strategy also returns 900.0 — different rules, same interface.
Negative amounts fail fast before the strategy runs.

mistakes.wrong: class Config { public static Config instance = new Config(); }
mistakes.right: private static final Config INSTANCE; private Config() { }
mistakes.why: A public mutable instance lets any code replace it, and a public constructor defeats the single-instance rule entirely.

mistakes.wrong: static List<Order> cache = new ArrayList<>(); // adds forever
mistakes.right: A bounded cache with eviction, or no static cache at all.
mistakes.why: A static collection is reachable forever, so the GC cannot reclaim it — the classic Java memory leak.

debug.brief: This singleton can be created more than once. Fix it so get() always returns the same instance.
hints: get() creates a new object on every call.
Store one instance statically and make the constructor private.

best: Name things for what they mean, not how they are stored.
Inject dependencies so behaviour can be tested without a database or network.
Use a pattern only when the problem it solves is actually present.
Measure performance with a profiler; do not guess.
modules.tip: Close the interview with a project you can defend: state the problem, the design, one trade-off you made, and the result. Interviewers remember a clear trade-off story far longer than a list of technologies.
revision: Stack per thread, heap shared, GC reclaims unreachable objects.
Patterns: singleton, factory, builder, strategy — know a real use for each.
JUnit asserts behaviour; Mockito supplies controlled collaborators.
A defensible capstone beats ten unfinished tutorials.

practice.title: Factory
practice.prompt: Write a NotificationFactory that returns Email or Sms implementations from a string, with an unknown-type fallback.
practice.hint: Return the interface type; throw for unknown input.

practice.title: Testable service
practice.prompt: Refactor a service that news up a repository to accept the repository through its constructor.
practice.hint: Then write a fake repository in main and assert the output.

practice.title: Complexity review
practice.prompt: Take one of your coding-bank solutions and state its time and space complexity with a one-line justification.
practice.hint: Count loop iterations and extra storage.

mcqs.q: Where do objects live in a running JVM?
mcqs.explain: Objects and arrays are allocated on the shared heap; frames and locals live on thread stacks.

mcqs.q: Which pattern swaps an algorithm behind an interface?
mcqs.explain: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface.

mcqs.q: What does a static collection usually cause in a long-running app?
mcqs.explain: It stays reachable forever, so its contents cannot be collected.

interview.q: How does garbage collection decide what to free?
interview.a: It starts from GC roots (stack references, static fields, JNI references) and marks everything reachable. Unreachable objects are reclaimed; modern collectors then compact or copy survivors. You cannot force a collection, and calling System.gc() is only a hint.
interview.followUp: Can Java leak memory? (Yes — unintended references such as static caches, listeners or ThreadLocals keep objects reachable.)

interview.q: How do you unit-test a class that talks to a database?
interview.a: Depend on an interface (repository) and inject it. In the test, pass a fake or a Mockito mock, then assert the service's behaviour and the interactions that matter. Integration tests cover the real SQL separately.
interview.followUp: What should a unit test avoid? (Real network, real database, sleeps and shared mutable state.)

questions.q: Which guarantees visibility across threads?
questions.explain: volatile establishes a happens-before edge for that variable.

questions.q: What is a race condition?
questions.explain: The result depends on interleaving of concurrent operations.

questions.q: How do you stop an ExecutorService gracefully?
questions.explain: shutdown stops new tasks; awaitTermination waits for completion.

questions.q: Which JDBC object prevents SQL injection?
questions.explain: PreparedStatement binds parameters rather than concatenating SQL.

questions.q: Which annotation makes a method an override checked by the compiler?
questions.explain: @Override verifies the signature matches a supertype method.

questions.q: Which design pattern ensures one instance?
questions.explain: Singleton controls construction so only one instance exists.

questions.q: What is the best first step when a Java service leaks memory?
questions.explain: Heap dumps identify what is still reachable and why.
